# Keys, nested keys, and locking

A tensordict groups related tensors in a tree. One key reads any of them: a
string for the top level, a tuple of strings for a nested entry. A lock fixes
the set of keys, so that no code adds, replaces, or removes an entry by
mistake.

## Nested tensordicts and nested keys

A key is a string. The value of an entry can be another TensorDict: the
constructor converts each nested dictionary into one, with the batch size of
the parent. This training batch has two levels:

```
>>> import torch
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict
>>> data = TensorDict(
... {
... "inputs": {
... "image": torch.rand(100, 28, 28),
... "mask": torch.randint(2, (100, 28, 28), dtype=torch.uint8),
... },
... "outputs": {"logits": torch.randn(100, 10)},
... },
... batch_size=[100],
... )
>>> type(data["inputs"]).__name__, data["inputs"].batch_size
('TensorDict', torch.Size([100]))
```

A nested key is a tuple of strings, and each string selects one level of the
tree. `data["a", "b"]` is the same as `data[("a", "b")]` and as
`data["a"]["b"]`. A write with a nested key creates the nested tensordicts
that do not exist yet:

```
>>> image = data["inputs", "image"]
>>> logits = data.get(("outputs", "logits"))
>>> data["outputs", "probabilities"] = torch.sigmoid(logits)
>>> data["extra", "count"] = torch.zeros(100)
>>> data["extra"].batch_size
torch.Size([100])
```

A tuple key in the constructor also creates nested entries:
`TensorDict({("x", "y"): torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3])` has a nested
tensordict `"x"` with the key `"y"`.

Keyword arguments are a shorthand for top-level keys:
`TensorDict(obs=torch.zeros(3), batch_size=[3])` is the same as
`TensorDict({"obs": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3])`. In the shorthand, the
names of the constructor arguments (`source`, `batch_size`, `device`,
`names`, `non_blocking`, and `lock`) are not keys, and a key must be a
Python identifier. A key such as `"obs.next"` or a tuple key needs the dict.
These docs build every TensorDict from a dict.

If you know the keys when you write the code, a
[`TensorClass`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass) gives you typed attributes in place of string
keys, and your editor completes them (see [TensorClass](../tensorclass.html#tensorclass-guide)).

## Valid keys

The type name [`NestedKey`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NestedKey.html#tensordict.NestedKey) covers the two forms of a key: a
string, or a tuple of strings. A tuple inside a tuple is flattened, and a
tuple of one string is the same as the string:

```
>>> from tensordict import unravel_key
>>> unravel_key(("a", ("b", "c")))
('a', 'b', 'c')
>>> unravel_key(("a",))
'a'
```

Any other key raises a `KeyError`. A string with a dot, such as `"a.b"`,
is one plain key, not a nested key.

```
>>> TensorDict().get(("a", 1))
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
KeyError: "Only NestedKeys are supported: a key must be a string or a non-empty, possibly nested tuple of strings. Got key ('a', 1)."
```

## List the keys

[`keys()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.keys.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.keys) lists the keys of the top level. Two
arguments change this:

- `include_nested=True` also lists the keys inside the nested tensordicts,
as tuples.
- `leaves_only=True` lists only the leaves. A leaf is an entry that is not a
tensordict, such as a tensor or a [`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData).

The keys come in insertion order. With `include_nested=True`, the keys inside
a nested tensordict come before the key of that tensordict. This robot state
has a timestamp, an arm, and a gripper on the arm:

```
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "time": torch.zeros(3),
... "arm": {"pos": torch.zeros(3), "gripper": {"force": torch.zeros(3)}},
... },
... batch_size=[3],
... )
>>> list(td.keys())
['time', 'arm']
>>> list(td.keys(include_nested=True))
['time', ('arm', 'pos'), ('arm', 'gripper', 'force'), ('arm', 'gripper'), 'arm']
>>> list(td.keys(include_nested=True, leaves_only=True))
['time', ('arm', 'pos'), ('arm', 'gripper', 'force')]
>>> list(td.keys(leaves_only=True))
['time']
```

[`values()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.values.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.values) and [`items()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.items.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.items)
take the same arguments.

To test a key, use `key in td`. It accepts nested keys. `key in td.keys()`
finds a nested key only with `include_nested=True`:

```
>>> ("arm", "pos") in td
True
>>> ("arm", "pos") in td.keys(include_nested=True)
True
>>> ("arm", "pos") in td.keys()
False
```

On a [`LazyStackedTensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict.html#tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict), a
[`TensorDictStore`](../reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore) and a
[`LazyStackedTensorDictStore`](../reference/generated/tensordict.store.LazyStackedTensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.LazyStackedTensorDictStore),
`("arm", "pos") in td.keys()` is `True` and emits a `FutureWarning`. This
result is deprecated and will be removed in TensorDict 0.17: from then on, the
check returns `False`.

On a [`TensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict), and on most other types,
`key in td.keys(include_nested=True, leaves_only=True)` checks that the key
exists, not that it is a leaf. A sub-tensordict is in the view, although
iterating the view does not list it (a
[`LazyStackedTensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict.html#tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict) and a
[`PersistentTensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.html#tensordict.PersistentTensorDict) check that the key is a leaf):

```
>>> "arm" in td.keys(include_nested=True, leaves_only=True)
True
>>> "arm" in list(td.keys(include_nested=True, leaves_only=True))
False
```

To test that a key is a leaf, pass the class of its entry to the `is_leaf`
function of the view, by default [`default_is_leaf()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.default_is_leaf.html#tensordict.default_is_leaf):

```
>>> from tensordict import default_is_leaf
>>> default_is_leaf(td.entry_class("arm"))
False
>>> default_is_leaf(td.entry_class(("arm", "pos")))
True
```

## Read an entry

`td[key]` and `td.get(key)` act differently on a missing key:

- `td[key]` raises a `KeyError`.
- `td.get(key)` returns `None`, as [`dict.get()`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict.get) does.
- `td.get(key, default)` returns `default`.

This is also true for a nested key, at any depth:

```
>>> td.get("missing") is None
True
>>> td.get(("arm", "missing"), torch.ones(3))
tensor([1., 1., 1.])
>>> td["missing"]
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
KeyError: 'key "missing" not found in TensorDict with keys [\'arm\', \'time\']'
```

`get` takes more arguments for lazy stacks whose entries have different
shapes. See [Variable-size data](stacking.html#stacking-variable-size).

## Write an entry

There are three ways to write a value under a key. They differ in what happens
to the tensor that is already there:

- `td[key] = value` and `td.set(key, value)` put `value` in the
tensordict. If the key exists, the old tensor is replaced, not changed. If
the key does not exist, it is added.
- `td.set(key, value, inplace=True)` copies `value` into the existing
tensor if the key exists. If the key does not exist, it is added.
- `td.set_(key, value)` copies `value` into the existing tensor. If the key
does not exist, it raises a `KeyError`.

For example:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"pos": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3])
>>> old = td["pos"]
>>> _ = td.set("pos", torch.ones(3))
>>> old # replaced: the old tensor did not change
tensor([0., 0., 0.])
>>> old = td["pos"]
>>> _ = td.set_("pos", torch.full((3,), 2.0))
>>> old # copied into the same tensor
tensor([2., 2., 2.])
>>> td.set_("vel", torch.zeros(3))
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
KeyError: 'key "vel" not found in TensorDict with keys [\'pos\']'
```

[In-place operations](operations.html#inplace-conventions) gives the rules for the other in-place operations.

## Write several entries

[`update()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.update.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.update) calls `set` for each entry of a
dictionary or a TensorDict. A nested dictionary updates the nested tensordict:
the keys that it does not give stay as they are. With `inplace=True`, it
copies into the existing tensors, as `set(..., inplace=True)` does.
[`update_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.update_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.update_) copies into existing tensors only, and
raises a `KeyError` for a missing key.

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"time": torch.zeros(3), "arm": {"pos": torch.zeros(3)}}, batch_size=[3])
>>> _ = td.update({"time": torch.ones(3), "arm": {"vel": torch.ones(3)}})
>>> list(td.keys(include_nested=True, leaves_only=True))
['time', ('arm', 'pos'), ('arm', 'vel')]
```

`update` writes the entries one after the other. If one entry raises, for
example on a batch size mismatch, the entries before it are already written.

## Select, exclude, and remove entries

[`select()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.select.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.select) returns a new tensordict with the keys
that you name. [`exclude()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.exclude.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.exclude) returns a new tensordict
without them. Both accept nested keys. They do not copy the tensors: the new
tensordict holds the same tensors as the original.

```
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "time": torch.zeros(3),
... "arm": {"pos": torch.zeros(3), "gripper": {"force": torch.zeros(3)}},
... },
... batch_size=[3],
... )
>>> list(td.select("time", ("arm", "pos")).keys(include_nested=True))
['time', ('arm', 'pos'), 'arm']
>>> list(td.exclude("time", ("arm", "gripper")).keys(include_nested=True))
[('arm', 'pos'), 'arm']
>>> td.select("time")["time"] is td["time"]
True
```

`select` raises a `KeyError` for a missing key, unless you pass
`strict=False`. `exclude` ignores missing keys. With `inplace=True`,
both change the tensordict and return it.

To remove one entry, use `del td[key]` or [`pop()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.pop.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.pop).
`pop(key)` raises a `KeyError` for a missing key, and `pop(key, default)`
returns `default`.

## Rename a key

[`rename_key_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.rename_key_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.rename_key_) renames a key in place and returns
the tensordict. The old and the new keys can be nested, and at different
levels:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"time": torch.zeros(3), "arm": {"pos": torch.zeros(3)}}, batch_size=[3])
>>> list(td.rename_key_(("arm", "pos"), "pos").keys(include_nested=True))
['time', 'arm', 'pos']
```

If the new key exists, `rename_key_` replaces its value. With
`safe=True`, it raises a `KeyError` instead. A new key inside the old one,
such as `("arm", "arm")` for `"arm"`, moves the entry there, as
`td.set(("arm", "arm"), td.pop("arm"))` does. Nothing is replaced, so
`safe=True` does not raise for it.

## Flatten and unflatten the keys

[`flatten_keys()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.flatten_keys.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.flatten_keys) returns a tensordict with one
level. It joins each nested key into one string, with `"."` as the default
separator. [`unflatten_keys()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.unflatten_keys.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.unflatten_keys) does the reverse.
The two methods do not copy the tensors. Use them for code or file formats
that accept only flat string keys.

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"time": torch.zeros(3), "arm": {"pos": torch.zeros(3)}}, batch_size=[3])
>>> flat = td.flatten_keys()
>>> list(flat.keys())
['time', 'arm.pos']
>>> list(flat.unflatten_keys().keys(include_nested=True))
['time', ('arm', 'pos'), 'arm']
>>> list(td.flatten_keys("/").keys())
['time', 'arm/pos']
```

## Locking and temporary changes

A locked tensordict does not accept a change to its keys. Code can still
change the values of the existing tensors.

### What a lock blocks

[`lock_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.lock_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.lock_) locks a tensordict and all its nested
tensordicts. A locked tensordict raises a `RuntimeError` for each of these
operations:

- Add a key, at any level.
- Replace an entry: `td[key] = value`, `set`, and `update` without
`inplace=True`.
- Remove or rename an entry: `del`, `pop`, `rename_key_`, and
`select` or `exclude` with `inplace=True`.

For example, a new key in a nested tensordict raises:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"time": torch.zeros(3), "arm": {"pos": torch.zeros(3)}}, batch_size=[3])
>>> _ = td.lock_()
>>> td["arm", "vel"] = torch.zeros(3)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: Cannot modify locked TensorDict. For in-place modification, consider using the `set_()` method and make sure the key is present.
```

These operations write into the existing entries, so they work on a locked
tensordict, for tensor and non-tensor entries alike:

- `set_` and `update_`.
- `set(..., inplace=True)` and `update(..., inplace=True)`, if the key
exists.
- An assignment to a batch index, such as `td[0] = other`.
- An in-place method of the tensordict, such as `td.add_(1)` or
`td.zero_()`, or of one tensor, such as `td["time"].add_(1)`.

For example:

```
>>> _ = td.set_("time", torch.ones(3))
>>> td["time"].add_(1)
tensor([2., 2., 2.])
```

`td["time"] += 1` raises on a locked tensordict, but only after it changed
the tensor. Python runs it as `td["time"] = td["time"].__iadd__(1)`: the
in-place add works, and the assignment then raises. Use
`td["time"].add_(1)` instead.

To read the lock state, use [`is_locked`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.is_locked.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.is_locked). To
remove it, call [`unlock_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.unlock_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.unlock_) on the root
tensordict. If you unlock a nested tensordict of a locked tensordict alone, it
raises a `RuntimeError`.

### Who locks a tensordict

You lock a tensordict with `lock_()` or with `TensorDict(..., lock=True)`.
These methods also lock it:

- [`memmap_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap_) locks the tensordict, and
[`memmap()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap) returns a locked tensordict.
[`load_memmap()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap) returns an unlocked tensordict.
- [`share_memory_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.share_memory_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.share_memory_) locks the tensordict (see
[Devices, dtypes, and memory](devices.html#devices)).
- [`consolidate()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate) returns a locked tensordict.
- [`tensordict.from_module()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.from_module.html#tensordict.from_module) returns a locked tensordict.
[`TensorDict.from_module`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict.from_module) returns an
unlocked one.

A new tensordict that a method returns is not always locked like the original.
On a locked tensordict, `clone()`, `select()`, `apply()`, indexing, and
[`torch.stack()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.stack.html#torch.stack) return an unlocked tensordict. `view()`, `reshape()`,
`unsqueeze()`, and `to()` return a locked one. Read `is_locked` on the
result if your code depends on it.

### Temporary changes with `with`

Some methods of a tensordict also work as context managers. At the end of the
`with` block, they undo their change.

`with td.unlock_():` unlocks the tensordict for the block, and locks it again
at the end. `with td.lock_():` does the reverse.

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"pos": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3], lock=True)
>>> with td.unlock_():
... td["vel"] = torch.ones(3)
>>> td.is_locked, sorted(td.keys())
(True, ['pos', 'vel'])
```

`with params.to_module(module):` puts the parameters and buffers of the
tensordict `params` into `module` for the block. At the end, the module
gets its original parameters back:

```
>>> from torch import nn
>>> module = nn.Linear(3, 2)
>>> params = TensorDict.from_module(module).clone()
>>> _ = params.zero_()
>>> with params.to_module(module):
... y = module(torch.ones(1, 3))
>>> y.detach()
tensor([[0., 0.]])
>>> bool((module.weight == 0).all())
False
```

`unlock_`, `lock_`, and `to_module` also undo their change when the
`with` block raises an exception.

These shape operations also work as context managers:
[`view()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.view.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.view), [`permute()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.permute.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.permute),
[`transpose()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.transpose.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.transpose),
[`unsqueeze()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.unsqueeze.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.unsqueeze),
[`flatten()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.flatten.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.flatten), and
[`unflatten()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.unflatten.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.unflatten). At the end of the block, the entries
that you wrote into the result go back into the original, with the reverse
operation. [`reshape()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.reshape.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.reshape) does not write back.
[`to()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.to.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.to) also writes back, and casts the existing
entries back to their original device and dtype (see
[Temporary moves](devices.html#devices-temporary-moves)). If the block raises an exception, these
operations write nothing back.

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"x": torch.zeros(3, 4)}, batch_size=[3, 4])
>>> with td.unsqueeze(-1) as tdu:
... tdu["y"] = torch.ones(3, 4, 1)
>>> td["y"].shape
torch.Size([3, 4])
```

[`get()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.get.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.get), [`set()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.set.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.set),
[`set_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.set_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.set_), and [`lock_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.lock_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.lock_)
in the [API reference](../reference/index.html#api-reference).

and locking.

# Non-tensor data and unbatched entries

A tensordict can store strings, labels, and other Python objects next to its
tensors. Indexing and stacking keep them aligned with the batch. A tensordict
can also hold a tensor that belongs to the whole batch, such as a parameter
that all the elements share. Shape operations leave that tensor as it is.

## Non-tensor data

In this example, each DNA read has a sequence and its GC content, the
fraction of G and C bases. A mask on the GC content selects the matching
sequences too:

```
>>> import torch
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict
>>> reads = TensorDict(
... {
... "seq": ["ACGT", "GGCC", "TTAG"],
... "gc": torch.tensor([0.50, 1.00, 0.25]),
... },
... batch_size=[3],
... )
>>> gc_rich = reads[reads["gc"] > 0.4]
>>> gc_rich.batch_size
torch.Size([2])
>>> gc_rich.get("seq").tolist()
['ACGT', 'GGCC']
```

Three classes hold values that are not tensors:

- [`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData) holds one value for the whole batch.
Indexing returns the same value.
- [`NonTensorStack`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack) holds one value for each element of
the batch. The list of sequences above becomes one.
- [`MetaData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.MetaData.html#tensordict.MetaData) holds one value for the whole batch, like
[`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData). Stacking gives one
[`MetaData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.MetaData.html#tensordict.MetaData) if all the values are the same Python object.

### What becomes a tensor

When you set a value that is not a tensor, tensordict converts it:

- Python numbers, booleans, NumPy arrays, and lists of numbers become
tensors. `True` becomes `tensor(True)`.
- A dict becomes a nested tensordict.
- A list of other values, such as strings, becomes a
[`NonTensorStack`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack) with one value for each item of the
list. If the tensordict has a batch size, the length of the list must be
the first batch dimension, or the tensordict raises a `RuntimeError`.
- Any other value, such as a string or `None`, becomes a
[`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData).

This example shows the type of each entry:

```
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from tensordict import MetaData, NonTensorData, NonTensorStack
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {"flag": True, "n": 3, "arr": np.zeros(2), "nums": [1, 2], "text": "hello", "words": ["x", "y"]}
... )
>>> for key in ["flag", "n", "arr", "nums", "text", "words"]:
... print(key, type(td.get(key)).__name__)
flag Tensor
n Tensor
arr Tensor
nums Tensor
text NonTensorData
words NonTensorStack
```

To keep a number or a boolean as a Python value, wrap it in
[`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData). To store a list as one value, and not as
one value for each element, use [`set_non_tensor()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.set_non_tensor.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.set_non_tensor)
or wrap the list in [`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData):

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"flag": NonTensorData(True)}, batch_size=[2])
>>> td["flag"]
True
>>> _ = td.set_non_tensor("labels", ["cat", "dog", "bird"])
>>> td[0]["labels"]
['cat', 'dog', 'bird']
```

In a tensordict without batch dimensions, a number or a boolean, as a Python or
a NumPy scalar, written over an existing [`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData)
entry also becomes a tensor, and the write emits a [`FutureWarning`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#FutureWarning).
Starting with TensorDict 0.17, the default will change to keeping it as
[`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData), like the entry it replaces
([#1199](https://github.com/pytorch/tensordict/issues/1199)).
In the same way, [`set_at_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.set_at_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.set_at_) casts a list or a
number written at an index of a non-tensor entry to a tensor, and emits a
[`FutureWarning`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#FutureWarning). Starting with TensorDict 0.17, the default will change
to storing it as non-tensor data
([#2522](https://github.com/pytorch/tensordict/issues/2522)).

`td[index] = value`, with a list or a number, writes the value into every
entry, and casts it to a tensor in the non-tensor entries too. The write emits a
[`FutureWarning`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#FutureWarning). Starting with TensorDict 0.17, the default will change
to leaving the non-tensor entries unchanged, as a
[`TensorDictStore`](../reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore) does for a number. To reset the
tensor entries of a tensordict with a string entry, for example:

```
td = TensorDict(x=torch.ones(3), name=NonTensorStack("a", "b", "c"), batch_size=[3])
td[mask] = 0
# today: td["x"][mask] is 0 and td["name"][mask] holds tensor(0), with a FutureWarning
# from 0.17: td["x"][mask] is 0 and td["name"] is still ["a", "b", "c"]
```

To leave the non-tensor entries unchanged now, write into
`td.exclude("name")[mask]`, which shares the tensors of `td`.

### Read a non-tensor entry

You can also create the [`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData) yourself. The
tensordict stores it like a tensor. Here, the entry records the reference
genome of the reads:

```
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "genome": NonTensorData("hg38"),
... "score": torch.zeros(()),
... },
... )
>>> print(td)
TensorDict(
 fields={
 genome: NonTensorData(data=hg38, batch_size=torch.Size([]), device=None),
 score: Tensor(shape=torch.Size([]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
```

Indexing with a key (`td["genome"]`) returns the content of the
[`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData). [`get()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.get.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.get)
returns the [`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData) object itself.
[`get_non_tensor()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.get_non_tensor.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.get_non_tensor) returns the content, as
`td["genome"]` does:

```
>>> print(td["genome"])
hg38
>>> print(td.get("genome"))
NonTensorData(data=hg38, batch_size=torch.Size([]), device=None)
>>> td.get_non_tensor("genome")
'hg38'
```

### One value for the batch, or one for each element

In a tensordict with a batch size, a [`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData)
gets the batch size of the tensordict:

```
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "genome": NonTensorData("hg38"),
... "score": torch.zeros(3),
... },
... batch_size=[3]
... )
>>> print(td)
TensorDict(
 fields={
 genome: NonTensorData(data=hg38, batch_size=torch.Size([3]), device=None),
 score: Tensor(shape=torch.Size([3]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([3]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
```

All the elements of the batch have the same value:

```
>>> print(td[0])
TensorDict(
 fields={
 genome: NonTensorData(data=hg38, batch_size=torch.Size([]), device=None),
 score: Tensor(shape=torch.Size([]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
```

If you write a different value into one element, the entry becomes a
[`NonTensorStack`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack):

```
>>> td[0] = TensorDict({"genome": "mm10", "score": torch.ones(())})
>>> type(td.get("genome")).__name__
'NonTensorStack'
```

When `td[index] = src` brings a non-tensor key that a dense `td` does not
have, a [`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData) in `src` (one value for the whole
batch) fills every row of `td`, written or not, while a
[`NonTensorStack`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack) (one value for each row) leaves `None` in
the rows that `index` does not select:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"score": torch.zeros(4)}, batch_size=[4])
>>> td[1:3] = TensorDict({"score": torch.ones(2), "genome": "hg38"}, batch_size=[2])
>>> td["genome"]
'hg38'
>>> td = TensorDict({"score": torch.zeros(4)}, batch_size=[4])
>>> td[1:3] = TensorDict(
... {"score": torch.ones(2), "seq": NonTensorStack("ACGT", "GGCC")}, batch_size=[2]
... )
>>> td.get("seq").tolist()
[None, 'ACGT', 'GGCC', None]
```

To give each element of the batch its own value, use a
[`NonTensorStack`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack):

```
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "seq": NonTensorStack("ACGT", "GGCC", "TTAG"),
... "score": torch.zeros(3),
... },
... batch_size=[3]
... )
>>> print(td)
TensorDict(
 fields={
 score: Tensor(shape=torch.Size([3]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False),
 seq: NonTensorStack(
 ['ACGT', 'GGCC', 'TTAG'],
 batch_size=torch.Size([3]),
 device=None)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([3]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
```

Index the tensordict to get one element. The first element has the first
sequence:

```
>>> print(td[0])
TensorDict(
 fields={
 score: Tensor(shape=torch.Size([]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False),
 seq: NonTensorData(data=ACGT, batch_size=torch.Size([]), device=None)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
```

For a stack, `td["seq"]` returns a `tensordict.utils.LinkedList`. It is a
subclass of [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list), and an assignment to one of its items writes into
the tensordict. [`tolist()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack.tolist) returns a plain
[`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list):

```
>>> values = td["seq"]
>>> isinstance(values, list)
True
>>> values[1] = "CCGG"
>>> td[1]["seq"]
'CCGG'
>>> td.get("seq").tolist()
['ACGT', 'CCGG', 'TTAG']
```

A [`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData) that holds a list does not give one
value for each element. A non-tensor value can be any Python object, so the
list is one value for the whole batch:

```
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "seq": NonTensorData(["ACGT", "GGCC", "TTAG"]),
... "score": torch.zeros(3),
... },
... batch_size=[3]
... )
>>> print(td[0])
TensorDict(
 fields={
 score: Tensor(shape=torch.Size([]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False),
 seq: NonTensorData(data=['ACGT', 'GGCC', 'TTAG'], batch_size=torch.Size([]), device=None)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
```

### Stacking tensordicts with non-tensor data

[`stack()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.stack.html#torch.stack) makes a [`NonTensorStack`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack) from
[`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData) entries, also if their values are the
same:

```
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "genome": NonTensorData("hg38"),
... "score": torch.zeros(()),
... },
... )
>>> print(torch.stack([td, td]))
TensorDict(
 fields={
 genome: NonTensorStack(
 ['hg38', 'hg38'],
 batch_size=torch.Size([2]),
 device=None),
 score: Tensor(shape=torch.Size([2]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([2]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
```

For [`MetaData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.MetaData.html#tensordict.MetaData) entries, [`stack()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.stack.html#torch.stack) returns one
[`MetaData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.MetaData.html#tensordict.MetaData) if all the stacked values are the same Python
object. It compares them with `is`, not with `==`. Otherwise, it returns
a [`NonTensorStack`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack), as for
[`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData):

```
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "genome": MetaData("hg38"),
... "score": torch.zeros(()),
... },
... )
>>> print(torch.stack([td, td]))
TensorDict(
 fields={
 genome: MetaData(data=hg38, batch_size=torch.Size([2]), device=None),
 score: Tensor(shape=torch.Size([2]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([2]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
>>> equal_lists = [TensorDict({"a": MetaData([1, 2])}), TensorDict({"a": MetaData([1, 2])})]
>>> type(torch.stack(equal_lists).get("a")).__name__
'NonTensorStack'
```

[`unsqueeze()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.unsqueeze.html#torch.unsqueeze) also keeps one [`MetaData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.MetaData.html#tensordict.MetaData), and
makes a [`NonTensorStack`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack) from a
[`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData). Use [`MetaData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.MetaData.html#tensordict.MetaData) for a
value that must not become a stack, such as a label or a configuration dict
that is the same for every element.

### Non-tensor data in other operations

- Arithmetic, [`apply()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply), and
[`to()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.to.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.to) pass non-tensor entries to the result as
they are. `==` and `!=` between two tensordicts compare them (see
[Arithmetic, apply, reductions, and gradients](operations.html#operations)).
- `keys(leaves_only=True)`, `values(leaves_only=True)`, and
`items(leaves_only=True)` skip the non-tensor entries. To include them,
pass `is_leaf=tensordict.is_leaf_nontensor`:

```
>>> from tensordict import is_leaf_nontensor
>>> td = TensorDict({"text": "x", "t": torch.zeros(())})
>>> list(td.keys(leaves_only=True))
['t']
>>> list(td.keys(leaves_only=True, is_leaf=is_leaf_nontensor))
['text', 't']
```
- Under [`torch.compile()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.compile.html#torch.compile), a function that returns a string entry
compiles again for each new string, and non-strict
[`torch.export.export()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/user_guide/torch_compiler/export/api_reference.html#torch.export.export) does not accept non-tensor entries. See
[torch.compile, torch.func, torch.export, and CUDA graphs](../compile.html#compile).
- [`share_memory_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.share_memory_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.share_memory_) can change non-tensor values
(see [Devices, dtypes, and memory](devices.html#devices)), and [`parse_tensor_dict_string()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.parse_tensor_dict_string.html#tensordict.parse_tensor_dict_string)
raises a `ValueError` for them (see [Printing and display](../printing.html#printing)).

## UnbatchedTensor

Warning

`UnbatchedTensor` is experimental: its API can change in a minor release
without a deprecation cycle.

Some tensors belong to the whole batch, not to each element: a configuration
tensor, a mask, or parameters that all the elements share. The shape of such
a tensor does not start with the batch size. To store it in a tensordict, wrap
it in an [`UnbatchedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.UnbatchedTensor.html#tensordict.UnbatchedTensor). In this example, 2 systems of 3
particles share one gravity vector:

```
>>> from tensordict import UnbatchedTensor
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "height": torch.randn(2, 3),
... "gravity": UnbatchedTensor(torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, -9.8])),
... },
... batch_size=[2, 3],
... )
```

Shape operations and indexing on the tensordict keep the storage of the
[`UnbatchedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.UnbatchedTensor.html#tensordict.UnbatchedTensor):

```
>>> reshaped = td.reshape(6)
>>> reshaped["gravity"].data_ptr() == td["gravity"].data_ptr()
True
>>> parts = td.unbind(0)
>>> parts[0]["gravity"].data_ptr() == parts[1]["gravity"].data_ptr()
True
>>> td[0]["gravity"].shape
torch.Size([3])
```

Pointwise arithmetic applies to the wrapped data:

```
>>> td2 = td * 2
>>> torch.equal(td2["gravity"], torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, -19.6]))
True
```

### Rules

[`UnbatchedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.UnbatchedTensor.html#tensordict.UnbatchedTensor) follows these rules:

- It is a tensor. The wrapped data is a real `torch.Tensor` and can be used
as one.
- Operations that change only the batch shape do not change it.
`reshape`, `view`, `unbind`, `split`, `squeeze`, `unsqueeze`,
`permute`, `transpose`, `flatten`, `unflatten`, `chunk`,
`expand`, `cat`, `stack`, and indexing return the same
[`UnbatchedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.UnbatchedTensor.html#tensordict.UnbatchedTensor), with the same storage.
- [`apply()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply) and
[`named_apply()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.named_apply.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.named_apply) with a `batch_size` (also
with `out=`) count as shape operations: the function is not called on an
[`UnbatchedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.UnbatchedTensor.html#tensordict.UnbatchedTensor), which keeps its data and takes the new
batch size. Without a `batch_size`, the function is called on it.
- Other operations work as for a tensor: device and dtype casts (`to`),
pointwise arithmetic (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`), `clone`, gradient
computation, and access by key.
- Python conversions follow PyTorch. `str()`, `bool()`, `int()`,
`float()`, `complex()`, and conversions to an integer index go to the
wrapped tensor.

For example, an [`UnbatchedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.UnbatchedTensor.html#tensordict.UnbatchedTensor) with one element
converts like a regular PyTorch tensor:

```
>>> int(UnbatchedTensor(torch.tensor([3])))
3
>>> f"{UnbatchedTensor(torch.tensor(1.25)):.1f}"
'1.2'
```

### Read an unbatched entry

For a plain tensordict, both [`get()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.get.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.get) and
`td[key]` return the [`UnbatchedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.UnbatchedTensor.html#tensordict.UnbatchedTensor) wrapper:

```
>>> type(td.get("gravity"))
<class 'tensordict._unbatched.UnbatchedTensor'>
>>> type(td["gravity"])
<class 'tensordict._unbatched.UnbatchedTensor'>
```

For a tensorclass, both attribute access and `get()` also return the
[`UnbatchedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.UnbatchedTensor.html#tensordict.UnbatchedTensor) wrapper (see [TensorClass](../tensorclass.html#tensorclass-guide)):

```
>>> from tensordict import TensorClass
>>> class Bodies(TensorClass):
... gravity: torch.Tensor
... height: torch.Tensor
>>> bodies = Bodies(
... gravity=UnbatchedTensor(torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, -9.8])),
... height=torch.randn(3),
... batch_size=[3],
... )
>>> type(bodies.gravity)
<class 'tensordict._unbatched.UnbatchedTensor'>
>>> type(bodies.get("gravity"))
<class 'tensordict._unbatched.UnbatchedTensor'>
```

### Limitations

- Memory-mapped serialization and consolidation do not support
[`UnbatchedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.UnbatchedTensor.html#tensordict.UnbatchedTensor) yet.
[`memmap()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap) and
[`consolidate()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate) raise `NotImplementedError`
when the tensordict contains one. [`torch.save()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.save.html#torch.save) keeps them.
- If you stack tensordicts whose [`UnbatchedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.UnbatchedTensor.html#tensordict.UnbatchedTensor)
entries have different data, the result keeps only the data of the first
one, and it warns.

## See also

- [tensorclass and non-tensor data](../reference/tc.html#api-tensorclass): the reference entries of
[`NonTensorData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData), [`NonTensorStack`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack),
[`MetaData`](../reference/generated/tensordict.MetaData.html#tensordict.MetaData), and [`UnbatchedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.UnbatchedTensor.html#tensordict.UnbatchedTensor).
- [Stacking and variable-size data](stacking.html#stacking): stacks of tensordicts, and variable-size data.
- [TensorClass](../tensorclass.html#tensorclass-guide): tensorclass fields that hold non-tensor values.
- [Save and load tensordicts](../saving.html#saving): how non-tensor entries are saved.

# Arithmetic, apply, reductions, and gradients

Arithmetic, [`torch`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/torch.html#module-torch) functions, and reductions on a tensordict apply to
every leaf in one call, and gradients flow through them. A leaf is a tensor at
the end of a key path (see [Keys, nested keys, and locking](keys.html#keys)). You write the computation once for
the whole group of tensors, and the result keeps the keys and the batch size
(see [Batch size, shapes, and indexing](batch_size.html#batch-size)).

A [`TensorClass`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass) has the same operations, so a method that
you write with them runs on one element or on a whole batch (see
[TensorClass](../tensorclass.html#tensorclass-guide)).

## Pointwise operations

A pointwise operation applies to each leaf and returns a new tensordict with
the same keys. The other operand can be a tensordict, a tensor, or a Python
number. In this example, a weather grid of 3 by 4 cells has a pressure and a
2-D wind velocity for each cell:

```
>>> import torch
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "pressure": torch.ones(3, 4),
... "wind": {"velocity": torch.ones(3, 4, 2)},
... },
... batch_size=[3, 4],
... )
>>> (td * 2 + td)["wind", "velocity"][0, 0]
tensor([3., 3.])
>>> (td - torch.ones(4)).batch_size
torch.Size([3, 4])
>>> (td > 0)["pressure"].dtype
torch.bool
```

The Python operators work as follows:

| Operators | Tensordict on the left | Tensordict on the right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` | yes | yes (`1 - td`, `2 / td`) |
| `**` | yes | no: `2 ** td` raises `NotImplementedError` |
| `%` | yes | no: `2 % td` raises `TypeError` |
| `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | yes | yes |
| `&`, `\|`, `^` | yes | yes |

Comparisons return a tensordict with `torch.bool` leaves. The unary
operators `-` and `~` and the function [`abs()`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#abs) also work.

`//` and `@` are not supported: they raise `TypeError`. To use them,
call [`apply()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply) (see below).

Most pointwise functions of [`torch`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/torch.html#module-torch) also have a tensordict method:
[`exp()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.exp.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.exp), [`sqrt()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.sqrt.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.sqrt),
[`clamp()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.clamp.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.clamp), [`sigmoid()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.sigmoid.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.sigmoid),
[`lerp()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.lerp.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.lerp), and many more. The methods with a trailing
underscore, such as [`add_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.add_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.add_), write into the
leaves (see In-place operations). [Pointwise math](../reference/td.html#api-methods-pointwise) lists
them all.

```
>>> TensorDict({"x": torch.tensor([-2.0, 0.5, 3.0])}).clamp(0, 1)["x"]
tensor([0.0000, 0.5000, 1.0000])
```

Arithmetic, the pointwise methods, and the comparisons `<`, `<=`, `>`,
and `>=` keep non-tensor entries, such as strings, as they are (see
[Non-tensor data and unbatched entries](non_tensor.html#non-tensor-data)). `==` and `!=` between two tensordicts also
compare the non-tensor values, and give a boolean tensor at their keys.

When it can, tensordict computes a pointwise operation with the fused
`torch._foreach_<op>` kernels, one call for all the leaves. The
[`torch.func`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/func.api.html#module-torch.func) transforms, such as [`torch.vmap()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.vmap.html#torch.vmap), have no batching
rule for the `_foreach` ops. Inside them, tensordict applies the operation
to one leaf at a time. Inside [`torch.compile()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.compile.html#torch.compile), `td * t` with a tensor `t` breaks
the graph: call `td.mul(t)` instead. [torch.compile, torch.func, torch.export, and CUDA graphs](../compile.html#compile) gives the details.

### Broadcasting with a tensor

A tensor operand is aligned with the batch dimensions of the tensordict, not
with the full shape of each leaf:

1. The batch size and the shape of the tensor broadcast together, aligned on
the right, as two tensor shapes do. The result has this broadcast batch
size.
2. For each leaf, the tensor gets trailing dimensions of size 1, so it
broadcasts over the feature dimensions of that leaf (the dimensions after
the batch dimensions).

In this example, `td.batch_size` is `(3, 4)` and `td["wind", "velocity"]`
has shape `(3, 4, 2)`. `td * t` multiplies
`td["wind", "velocity"][i, j, k]` by `t[j]`:

```
>>> t = torch.arange(4.0)
>>> (td * t)["wind", "velocity"][1, 2]
tensor([2., 2.])
```

A tensor with more dimensions than the batch size gives a result with a
larger batch size:

```
>>> (td * torch.ones(2, 3, 4)).batch_size
torch.Size([2, 3, 4])
```

A tensor that matches only the feature dimensions does not broadcast. Its
shape must broadcast with the batch size:

```
>>> td * torch.ones(2)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: Attempting to broadcast a dimension of length 2 at -1! ...
```

To scale the feature dimensions, use `td.apply(lambda x: x * w)`.
In-place operators, such as `td *= t`, follow the same rules.

### Broadcasting between tensordicts

The batch sizes of two tensordicts must broadcast, aligned on the right.
Batch sizes `(3,)` and `(3, 4)` do not broadcast, even if the leaves have
the same shape:

```
>>> td2 = TensorDict({"a": torch.ones(3, 4)}, batch_size=[3])
>>> TensorDict({"a": torch.ones(3, 4)}, batch_size=[3, 4]) + td2
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: Attempting to broadcast a dimension of length 3 at -1! ...
```

If the two batch sizes have a different number of dimensions, the shape of
the leaves in the result can depend on the order of the operands:

```
>>> td0 = TensorDict({"x": torch.ones(3, 2)}, batch_size=[])
>>> td1 = TensorDict({"x": torch.ones(3, 2)}, batch_size=[3])
>>> (td1 + td0)["x"].shape
torch.Size([3, 2])
>>> (td0 + td1)["x"].shape
torch.Size([3, 3, 2])
```

`td0 + td1` follows the batch rules: `td0` has no batch dimensions, so
its entry is used for each of the 3 elements of `td1`, as with
`td0.expand(3)`. `td1 + td0` broadcasts the two leaves as plain tensors.
To get the same result in both orders, give the two tensordicts the same
batch size first, for example with [`expand()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.expand.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.expand):

```
>>> (td1 + td0.expand(3))["x"].shape
torch.Size([3, 3, 2])
```

### Missing entries

An operator between two tensordicts needs the same keys on both sides.
Otherwise it raises a `KeyError`. The methods
[`add()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.add.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.add), [`sub()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.sub.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.sub),
[`mul()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.mul.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.mul), [`div()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.div.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.div),
[`pow()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.pow.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.pow), [`maximum()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.maximum.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.maximum),
[`minimum()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.minimum.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.minimum),
[`clamp_max()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.clamp_max.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.clamp_max), and
[`clamp_min()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.clamp_min.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.clamp_min) accept a `default` keyword
argument for tensordicts with different keys:

- `default=None` (the default): the key sets must be the same.
- `default="intersection"`: the result has only the keys of both
tensordicts.
- A tensor, such as `default=torch.tensor(0.0)`: the tensor replaces each
missing entry, on both sides. A Python number (`default=0`) raises a
`TypeError`.

In this example, `x` and `y` share only the key `"a"`:

```
>>> x = TensorDict({"a": torch.ones(2), "b": torch.ones(2)}, batch_size=[2])
>>> y = TensorDict({"a": torch.ones(2), "c": torch.ones(2)}, batch_size=[2])
>>> x + y
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
KeyError: 'b'
>>> list(x.add(y, default="intersection").keys())
['a']
>>> sorted(x.add(y, default=torch.tensor(0.0)).keys())
['a', 'b', 'c']
```

## Apply a function to each leaf

[`apply()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply) calls a function on each leaf and
returns a new tensordict with the results, at the same keys. Use it for an
operation that has no tensordict method:

```
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "pressure": torch.ones(3, 4),
... "wind": {"velocity": torch.ones(3, 4, 2)},
... },
... batch_size=[3, 4],
... )
>>> td.apply(lambda x: x // 2)["pressure"][0]
tensor([0., 0., 0., 0.])
```

The function gets tensors only. Non-tensor entries go to the result as they
are. These arguments change what `apply` does:

- Other tensordicts after the function: `td.apply(fn, other)` calls
`fn(x, y)` with the leaves of `td` and `other` at the same key. If
`other` has no entry at a key, `apply` raises a `KeyError`, unless you
give `default=`.
- `batch_size=`: if the function changes the batch dimensions, give the new
batch size.
- A function that returns `None` for a leaf drops that entry from the
result.
- `inplace=True`, or [`apply_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply_): write the
results into the existing leaves and return the same tensordict.
- `out=`: write the results into another tensordict.

The next examples use another tensordict, `batch_size=`, and a function that
returns `None`:

```
>>> td.apply(lambda x, y: x + y, td)["pressure"][0, 0]
tensor(2.)
>>> td.apply(lambda x: x.sum(-1), batch_size=[3]).batch_size
torch.Size([3])
>>> list(td.apply(lambda x: x if x.ndim == 2 else None).keys(True, True))
['pressure']
```

[`named_apply()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.named_apply.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.named_apply) also passes the key to the
function, as its first argument. By default, the key is the last string of the
key path. With `nested_keys=True`, it is the full key, a tuple for a nested
entry:

```
>>> calm = td.named_apply(lambda key, x: x * 0 if key == "velocity" else x)
>>> calm["wind", "velocity"][0, 0, 0]
tensor(0.)
>>> _ = td.named_apply(lambda key, x: print(key), nested_keys=True)
pressure
('wind', 'velocity')
```

## Reductions

The reductions of [`torch`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/torch.html#module-torch) are tensordict methods too:
[`sum()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.sum.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.sum), [`mean()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.mean.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.mean),
[`std()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.std.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.std), [`var()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.var.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.var),
[`prod()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.prod.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.prod), [`min()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.min.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.min),
[`max()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.max.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.max), [`amin()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.amin.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.amin),
[`amax()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.amax.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.amax), [`nansum()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.nansum.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.nansum),
[`nanmean()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.nanmean.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.nanmean),
[`quantile()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.quantile.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.quantile),
[`logsumexp()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.logsumexp.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.logsumexp), [`norm()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.norm.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.norm),
[`all()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.all.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.all), and [`any()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.any.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.any).
The `dim` argument selects what they reduce:

- No `dim`: each leaf is reduced to one value. The result has batch size
`[]`.
- `dim=0`, `dim=-1`, or a tuple: these are batch dimensions. Each leaf is
reduced over them, and they are removed from the batch size of the result.
A `dim` that is not a batch dimension raises an `IndexError`.
- `dim="feature"`: each leaf is reduced over its feature dimensions. The
result keeps the batch size.

With `reduce=True`, the reduction also combines the leaves, and the result
is one tensor:

```
>>> td.sum()["wind", "velocity"]
tensor(24.)
>>> td.sum(dim=0)["wind", "velocity"].shape
torch.Size([4, 2])
>>> td.sum(dim="feature")["wind", "velocity"].shape
torch.Size([3, 4])
>>> td.sum(reduce=True)
tensor(36.)
>>> td.sum(dim="feature", reduce=True).shape
torch.Size([3, 4])
```

[`min()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.min.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.min) and [`max()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.max.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.max)
with a `dim` return a named tuple of two tensordicts, `values` and
`indices`, as [`torch.max()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.max.html#torch.max) does. [`all()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.all.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.all)
and [`any()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.any.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.any) without `dim` return a Python
`bool`:

```
>>> td.max(dim=0).indices["pressure"].dtype
torch.int64
>>> (td == 1).all()
True
```

## In-place operations

tensordict has two kinds of in-place operation:

- A method with a trailing underscore (`method_`), such as
[`add_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.add_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.add_), [`mul_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.mul_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.mul_),
or [`masked_fill_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.masked_fill_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.masked_fill_), writes into the same tensor
storage for every leaf. The `data_ptr` of each leaf does not change. This
is the convention of PyTorch. These methods exist only for operations that
keep the shape, dtype, and layout of each tensor.
- The `inplace=True` keyword of a shape-changing operation, such as
[`pad()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.pad.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.pad), [`repeat()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.repeat.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.repeat),
[`gather()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.gather.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.gather), or
[`repeat_interleave()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.repeat_interleave.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.repeat_interleave), keeps the tensordict
object and its keys. Each leaf can get a new tensor. The operation
allocates no second tensordict, and it releases each old leaf as soon as it
writes the new one. Peak memory therefore stays close to `1x`, not
`2x`. A shape-changing operation can offer only this kind of in-place.

In short, `method_` keeps the bytes, and `inplace=True` on a
shape-changing operation keeps the container.

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"a": torch.ones(3, 4)}, batch_size=[3, 4])
>>> ptr = td["a"].data_ptr()
>>> _ = td.add_(1)
>>> td["a"].data_ptr() == ptr
True
>>> padded = td.pad([0, 1], inplace=True)
>>> padded is td, td.batch_size, td["a"].data_ptr() == ptr
(True, torch.Size([4, 4]), False)
```

For [`set()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.set.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.set), [`update()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.update.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.update),
and [`apply()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply), `inplace=True` writes into the
existing leaf when the key exists, so its `data_ptr` does not change. A
value of another dtype is cast to the dtype of the leaf. `set()` and
`update()` add a missing key, and [`set_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.set_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.set_) and
[`update_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.update_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.update_) raise a `KeyError` for it (see
[Write an entry](keys.html#keys-write)).

```
>>> ptr = td["a"].data_ptr()
>>> _ = td.set("a", torch.zeros(4, 4), inplace=True)
>>> td["a"].data_ptr() == ptr
True
>>> td.set_("missing", torch.zeros(4, 4))
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
KeyError: 'key "missing" not found in TensorDict with keys ...
```

These methods follow neither of the two kinds:

- [`memmap_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap_) and
[`share_memory_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.share_memory_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.share_memory_) have a trailing underscore,
but they move each leaf to new storage: memory-mapped files, or shared
memory. The `data_ptr` of each leaf changes, and the tensordict gets
locked (see [Locking and temporary changes](keys.html#keys-locking)). For the same reason,
[`pin_memory_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.pin_memory_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.pin_memory_) is deprecated: use
`pin_memory(inplace=True)`.
- [`lock_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.lock_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.lock_), [`unlock_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.unlock_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.unlock_),
[`rename_key_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.rename_key_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.rename_key_), [`del_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.del_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.del_),
[`auto_batch_size_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.auto_batch_size_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.auto_batch_size_),
[`auto_device_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.auto_device_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.auto_device_), and
[`clear_device_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.clear_device_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.clear_device_) change the tensordict
itself: its lock, its keys, its batch size, or its device. They do not
touch the leaves.
- On the key methods [`select()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.select.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.select),
[`exclude()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.exclude.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.exclude), and
[`split_keys()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.split_keys.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.split_keys), `inplace=True` removes the
other keys from the tensordict and returns it. On
[`flatten_keys()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.flatten_keys.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.flatten_keys) and
[`unflatten_keys()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.unflatten_keys.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.unflatten_keys), it renames the keys of the
tensordict and returns it.
- On [`reshape()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.reshape.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.reshape),
[`flatten()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.flatten.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.flatten),
[`unflatten()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.unflatten.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.unflatten), and
[`contiguous()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.contiguous.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.contiguous), `inplace=True` keeps the
object, as for the other shape-changing operations. A leaf keeps its
storage when the operation can return a view of it.

For example, `select(inplace=True)` returns the same tensordict, with fewer
keys:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"a": torch.ones(2), "b": TensorDict({"c": torch.ones(2)})})
>>> td.select("a", inplace=True) is td, list(td.keys())
(True, ['a'])
```

## Gradients

Tensordicts work with [`torch.autograd`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/autograd.html#module-torch.autograd): a leaf that requires gradients
keeps its graph through the operations above.

### `torch.autograd.grad`

[`torch.autograd.grad()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.autograd.grad.html#torch.autograd.grad) accepts tensordicts, also nested ones, for its
`outputs`, `inputs`, and `grad_outputs`. tensordict passes the leaves to
PyTorch as tuples, and returns the gradients as a new tensordict with the
keys of `inputs`:

```
>>> inputs = TensorDict({"a": torch.ones(2, 3, requires_grad=True)})
>>> outputs = inputs * 2.0
>>> grads = torch.autograd.grad(outputs, inputs, torch.ones_like(outputs))
>>> grads["a"]
tensor([[2., 2., 2.],
 [2., 2., 2.]])
```

`outputs` and `inputs` must each be one tensordict. A tensor output with
tensordict inputs raises `ValueError: torch.autograd.grad for TensorDict
only supports TensorDictBase as output`. To differentiate a scalar loss,
put it in a tensordict:

```
>>> params = TensorDict({"w": torch.ones(3, requires_grad=True)})
>>> loss = (params["w"] ** 2).sum()
>>> torch.autograd.grad(TensorDict({"loss": loss}), params)["w"]
tensor([2., 2., 2.])
```

This also works for a module that reads and writes tensordicts, such as a
[`TensorDictModule`](../reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule) (see [Modules: TensorDictModule and tensordict.nn](../modules.html#modules-guide)). Select
the output keys of the module, so that the inputs are not part of the
outputs:

```
>>> from tensordict.nn import TensorDictModule
>>> _ = torch.manual_seed(0)
>>> module = TensorDictModule(torch.nn.Linear(3, 2), in_keys=["x"], out_keys=["y"])
>>> td_in = TensorDict({"x": torch.randn(4, 3, requires_grad=True)}, batch_size=[4])
>>> td_out = module(td_in.clone()).select(*module.out_keys)
>>> grads = torch.autograd.grad(td_out, td_in, torch.ones_like(td_out))
>>> grads["x"].shape
torch.Size([4, 3])
```

### `TensorDict.backward`

[`backward()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.backward.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.backward) works like
[`torch.Tensor.backward()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.Tensor.backward.html#torch.Tensor.backward). It collects the differentiable leaves of the
tensordict, also nested ones, and backpropagates through all of them in one
[`torch.autograd.backward()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.autograd.backward.html#torch.autograd.backward) call. If every leaf is a scalar, you do not
need to give a gradient. The usual case is a tensordict of losses, here a fit term and a
regularization term:

```
>>> w = torch.ones(3, requires_grad=True)
>>> loss_td = TensorDict({"fit_loss": (w ** 2).sum(), "reg_loss": w.sum()})
>>> loss_td.backward() # same as loss_td.sum(reduce=True).backward()
>>> w.grad
tensor([3., 3., 3.])
```

For leaves that are not scalars, or to weight each loss, pass a gradient
tensordict whose entries match the differentiable leaves by nested key:

```
>>> w.grad = None
>>> loss_td = TensorDict({"fit_loss": (w ** 2).sum(), "reg_loss": w.sum()})
>>> weights = TensorDict({"fit_loss": torch.tensor(0.5), "reg_loss": torch.tensor(1.0)})
>>> loss_td.backward(weights)
>>> w.grad
tensor([2., 2., 2.])
```

### Jacobians and Hessians

[`torch.func.jacrev()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.jacrev.html#torch.func.jacrev), [`torch.func.jacfwd()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.jacfwd.html#torch.func.jacfwd), and
[`torch.func.hessian()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.hessian.html#torch.func.hessian) work on functions that take and return
tensordicts. The result is a tensordict in which the entry
`J["output_key", "input_key"]` is the Jacobian block for that pair of keys:

```
>>> from torch.func import jacrev
>>> _ = torch.manual_seed(0)
>>> td = TensorDict({"a": torch.randn(3, 2), "b": torch.randn(3, 4)}, batch_size=[3])
>>> def f(td):
... return TensorDict(
... {"x": td["a"] ** 2, "y": td["b"] ** 3}, batch_size=td.batch_size
... )
>>> J = jacrev(f)(td)
>>> J.batch_size # preserved from input/output
torch.Size([3])
>>> J["x", "a"].shape # output_shape + input_shape = (3, 2) + (3, 2)
torch.Size([3, 2, 3, 2])
```

The three transforms can fail if the batch size is not empty and each leaf
has one element for each batch element. Examples are the shapes `(4,)` and
`(4, 1)` with `batch_size=[4]`. In this case, [`jacrev()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.jacrev.html#torch.func.jacrev)
works only if the function returns two or more keys.
[`jacfwd()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.jacfwd.html#torch.func.jacfwd) and [`hessian()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.hessian.html#torch.func.hessian) fail for any number
of keys. The errors are `RuntimeError: Expected pytree structure ...` and
`RuntimeError: jvp(f, primals, tangents): Expected primals and tangents to
have the same python structure ...`.

```
>>> def g(td):
... return TensorDict({"x": td["a"] ** 2}, batch_size=td.batch_size)
>>> jacrev(g)(TensorDict({"a": torch.randn(4)}, batch_size=[4]))
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: Expected pytree structure of cotangents to be the same as pytree structure of outputs to the function...
```

To avoid the error, do one of these:

- Set `batch_size=[]`, so that all the dimensions are feature dimensions.
- Give the leaves a feature dimension of size 2 or more. A dimension of
size 1 (`torch.randn(4, 1)`) does not help.

With `batch_size=[]`, the same function works:

```
>>> jacrev(g)(TensorDict({"a": torch.randn(4)}, batch_size=[]))["x", "a"].shape
torch.Size([4, 4])
```

[`torch.func`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/func.api.html#module-torch.func) also has [`torch.func.grad()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.grad.html#torch.func.grad) and [`torch.vmap()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.vmap.html#torch.vmap)
for tensordicts. [torch.compile, torch.func, torch.export, and CUDA graphs](../compile.html#compile) explains how they work with tensordicts, and
how to compute per-sample gradients and model ensembles.
