# Stacking and variable-size data

[`torch.stack()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.stack.html#torch.stack) and [`torch.cat()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.cat.html#torch.cat) join tensordicts as they join
tensors, so a list of samples becomes one batch in one call. A lazy stack also
joins tensordicts whose keys or shapes differ, such as graphs with different
numbers of nodes or sequences of different lengths.

## Dense stacking: torch.stack and torch.cat

[`torch.stack()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.stack.html#torch.stack) puts tensordicts along a new batch dimension.
[`torch.cat()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.cat.html#torch.cat) joins them along an existing batch dimension. Here, each
tensordict holds the 3-D positions of 2 particles:

```
>>> import torch
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict
>>> a = TensorDict({"pos": torch.zeros(2, 3)}, batch_size=[2])
>>> b = TensorDict({"pos": torch.ones(2, 3)}, batch_size=[2])
>>> stacked = torch.stack([a, b])
>>> type(stacked).__name__, stacked.batch_size
('TensorDict', torch.Size([2, 2]))
>>> torch.stack([a, b], dim=1)["pos"].shape
torch.Size([2, 2, 3])
>>> torch.cat([a, b]).batch_size
torch.Size([4])
```

Both return a regular [`TensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict), with one new tensor for
each key. This is a dense stack: it copies the data, so a later change to the
result does not change the inputs. [`tensordict.stack()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.stack.html#tensordict.stack) and
[`tensordict.cat()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.cat.html#tensordict.cat) are the same functions.

`torch.stack` raises a `RuntimeError` if the tensordicts do not have the
same keys, the same batch size, and the same shape for each entry.
`torch.cat` accepts different sizes along the joined dimension, but it
raises a `KeyError` if the keys differ:

```
>>> c = TensorDict({"pos": torch.zeros(2, 2)}, batch_size=[2]) # 2-D positions
>>> torch.stack([a, c])
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: The shapes of the tensors to stack is incompatible: torch.Size([2, 2]) vs torch.Size([2, 3]) for key pos.
>>> torch.stack([a, TensorDict({"vel": torch.zeros(2, 3)}, batch_size=[2])])
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: The sets of keys in the tensordicts to stack are exclusive. Consider using `LazyStackedTensorDict.maybe_dense_stack` instead.
```

For tensordicts that differ in these ways, use a lazy stack.

## Lazy stacks

A lazy stack is a [`LazyStackedTensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict.html#tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict). It keeps the list
of the original tensordicts, and it stacks their entries only when you read
them. [`lazy_stack()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.lazy_stack.html#tensordict.lazy_stack) always returns one. In this example, each
tensordict holds 10 time steps of one robot:

```
>>> from tensordict import lazy_stack
>>> tds = [
... TensorDict({"battery": torch.zeros(10), "joints": torch.zeros(10, 4)}, batch_size=[10])
... for _ in range(3)
... ]
>>> stacked = lazy_stack(tds) # no data is stacked here
>>> type(stacked).__name__, stacked.batch_size
('LazyStackedTensorDict', torch.Size([3, 10]))
>>> stacked["battery"].shape # stacks the "battery" entries only
torch.Size([3, 10])
```

You also get a lazy stack from [`torch.stack()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.stack.html#torch.stack) or [`torch.cat()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.cat.html#torch.cat) of lazy
stacks, and from [`maybe_dense_stack()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.maybe_dense_stack.html#tensordict.maybe_dense_stack) if the inputs cannot
make a dense stack. The table in Which function to use lists each
case.

### Read and write a lazy stack

A lazy stack reads and writes the original tensordicts:

- An index along the stack dimension returns the original tensordict.
- A write of an entry, or an in-place change, goes to the original
tensordicts. A new key goes to each of them.
- Any other index returns a new lazy stack, for example `stacked[:, 0]`.

For example:

```
>>> stacked[0] is tds[0]
True
>>> stacked["battery"] = torch.ones(3, 10)
>>> tds[0]["battery"].sum()
tensor(10.)
```

Each read of an entry stacks the values again, and allocates a new tensor. If
you read the same keys many times, call
[`contiguous()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.contiguous.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.contiguous) once and read from its
result. `contiguous()` returns a regular TensorDict that owns its data, so a
write to it does not change the original tensordicts:

```
>>> dense = stacked.contiguous()
>>> type(dense).__name__
'TensorDict'
>>> dense["battery"] += 1
>>> tds[0]["battery"].sum() # not changed
tensor(10.)
```

[`to_tensordict()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_tensordict.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_tensordict) does the same.
`contiguous()` raises a `RuntimeError` if the stacked entries have
different shapes. See Variable-size data for that case.

A lazy stack can name its stack dimension, with `stack_dim_name` in
[`lazy_stack()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.lazy_stack.html#tensordict.lazy_stack), or by setting its `names`. If the stacked
tensordicts have no names, `contiguous()`, `to_tensordict()` and
[`pad()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.pad.html#tensordict.pad) give a TensorDict without that name. `clone()`,
which returns a lazy stack, and
[`densify()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.densify.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.densify) keep it. To keep it in a
TensorDict, call `densify()`, or name the dimension again with
[`refine_names()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.refine_names.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.refine_names):

```
>>> named = lazy_stack(tds, stack_dim_name="robot")
>>> named.names
['robot', None]
>>> named.contiguous().names
[None, None]
>>> named.contiguous().refine_names("robot", ...).names
['robot', None]
>>> named.densify().names
['robot', None]
>>> named.clone().names
['robot', None]
```

If the stacked tensordicts have names, all of these methods keep every name.

Note

Only stacking is lazy. Shape operations such as `squeeze`, `unsqueeze`,
`permute`, and `view` return a regular TensorDict. The legacy lazy
versions of these operations exist only with
[`set_lazy_legacy()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.set_lazy_legacy.html#tensordict.set_lazy_legacy) set to `True`. This mode is deprecated
and will be removed in tensordict 0.17.

### Different keys and batch sizes

A lazy stack accepts tensordicts with different keys. The keys that are not in
every tensordict are exclusive keys. `keys()` does not list them, and you
cannot read them from the stack. Read them from one tensordict of the stack
instead:

```
>>> mixed = lazy_stack([
... TensorDict({"pos": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3]),
... TensorDict({"pos": torch.zeros(3), "charge": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3]),
... ])
>>> list(mixed.keys())
['pos']
>>> mixed[1]["charge"].shape
torch.Size([3])
```

A lazy stack also accepts tensordicts with different batch sizes, if they have
the same number of batch dimensions. The batch size then shows `-1` for each
dimension that differs. Here, two systems have 2 and 4 particles:

```
>>> ragged = lazy_stack([
... TensorDict({"pos": torch.zeros(2, 3)}, batch_size=[2]),
... TensorDict({"pos": torch.zeros(4, 3)}, batch_size=[4]),
... ])
>>> ragged.batch_size
torch.Size([2, -1])
>>> ragged[1].batch_size
torch.Size([4])
```

## Which function to use

The table gives the type that each function returns, for a list of two
tensordicts of each kind. "Lazy stack" means a
[`LazyStackedTensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict.html#tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict), and "raises" means that the
function raises an error.

| Inputs | `torch.stack` | `lazy_stack` | `maybe_dense_stack` | `torch.cat` | `pad_sequence` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Same keys and shapes | `TensorDict` | lazy stack | `TensorDict` | `TensorDict` | `TensorDict` |
| Entry shapes differ | raises | lazy stack | lazy stack | raises | raises, unless only the `pad_dim` dimension differs |
| Keys differ | raises | lazy stack | lazy stack | raises `KeyError` | raises `TypeError` |
| Batch sizes differ (same number of dimensions) | raises | lazy stack, `-1` in the batch size | lazy stack, `-1` in the batch size | `TensorDict` | `TensorDict` (padded) |
| Tensorclass instances | the tensorclass | the tensorclass | the tensorclass | the tensorclass | the tensorclass |
| Lazy stacks | lazy stack | lazy stack | lazy stack | lazy stack | `TensorDict` |

Use these rules to choose:

- If the inputs always have the same keys and shapes, use `torch.stack`. It
gives a regular TensorDict: a read returns the stored tensor, without a new
stack.
- If you must write back into the inputs, or if the keys or shapes can differ,
use `lazy_stack`.
- If the inputs usually match but sometimes do not, use
`maybe_dense_stack`. It gives a dense stack when it can, and a lazy stack
otherwise.

## Variable-size data

Some data does not have the same shape for each element: sequences of
different lengths, graphs with different numbers of nodes, strings. A dense
TensorDict cannot hold it, because each entry is one tensor.

### Lazy stacks

A lazy stack holds tensordicts whose entries have different shapes. The shape
of such an entry shows `-1` for each dimension that differs. `stacked[key]`
then raises a `RuntimeError`. To read the entry, pass one of these keyword
arguments to [`get()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.get.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.get):

- `as_list=True` returns a list with one tensor for each element.
- `as_padded_tensor=True` returns one tensor, padded to the longest element.
Set the padding with `padding_value` (default `0.0`) and
`padding_side` (`"right"` or `"left"`).
- `as_nested_tensor=True` returns a nested tensor ([`torch.nested`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/nested.html#module-torch.nested)). The
default layout is `torch.jagged`. Set another one with `layout`.

A dense tensordict returns the stored tensor for `as_list=True` and
`as_nested_tensor=True`, and warns. Starting with TensorDict 0.17, the
default will change to returning `list(tensor.unbind(0))` and a nested
tensor, as a lazy stack does.

For example, with three graphs of 2, 3, and 1 nodes, and 2 features for each
node:

```
>>> _ = torch.manual_seed(0)
>>> graphs = lazy_stack([TensorDict({"nodes": torch.randn(n, 2)}) for n in [2, 3, 1]])
>>> graphs
LazyStackedTensorDict(
 fields={
 nodes: Tensor(shape=torch.Size([3, -1, 2]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False)},
 exclusive_fields={
 },
 batch_size=torch.Size([3]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False,
 stack_dim=0)
>>> [t.shape for t in graphs.get("nodes", as_list=True)]
[torch.Size([2, 2]), torch.Size([3, 2]), torch.Size([1, 2])]
>>> graphs.get("nodes", as_padded_tensor=True).shape
torch.Size([3, 3, 2])
>>> graphs.get("nodes", as_nested_tensor=True).is_nested
True
>>> graphs[1]["nodes"].shape
torch.Size([3, 2])
```

[`densify()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.densify.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.densify) turns the whole lazy stack
into a regular TensorDict. The entries with different shapes become nested
tensors. Pass `layout=torch.jagged`: the default, `torch.strided`, gives a
warning from PyTorch, which recommends the jagged layout.

```
>>> dense = graphs.densify(layout=torch.jagged)
>>> type(dense).__name__, dense["nodes"].is_nested
('TensorDict', True)
```

A TensorDict can also hold a nested tensor with the `torch.jagged` layout
directly. Its first dimension is a batch dimension:

```
>>> nt = torch.nested.nested_tensor([torch.ones(2, 2), torch.ones(3, 2)], layout=torch.jagged)
>>> data = TensorDict({"nodes": nt}, batch_size=[2])
>>> data[1]["nodes"].shape
torch.Size([3, 2])
```

### Padding with pad_sequence

[`pad_sequence()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.pad_sequence.html#tensordict.pad_sequence) pads the entries of a list of tensordicts to
the longest one along `pad_dim`, and stacks them. With `return_mask=True`,
it adds a `"masks"` entry that marks the values that are not padding. Use it
to get one dense TensorDict, for example for a model that takes a padded
batch. Here, three recordings of a 2-channel sensor have 2, 3, and 1 samples:

```
>>> from tensordict import pad_sequence
>>> tds = [TensorDict({"signal": torch.ones(n, 2)}) for n in [2, 3, 1]]
>>> padded = pad_sequence(tds, return_mask=True)
>>> padded["signal"].shape
torch.Size([3, 3, 2])
>>> padded["masks", "signal"]
tensor([[ True, True, False],
 [ True, True, True],
 [ True, False, False]])
```

Pass `padding_side="left"` to put the padding before the data instead.
[`unpad_sequence()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.unpad_sequence.html#tensordict.unpad_sequence) goes back: it reads the masks and returns
a lazy stack of the samples, each with its own length:

```
>>> from tensordict import unpad_sequence
>>> samples = unpad_sequence(padded)
>>> [sample["signal"].shape for sample in samples.tensordicts]
[torch.Size([2, 2]), torch.Size([3, 2]), torch.Size([1, 2])]
```

`pad_sequence` raises a `RuntimeError` for 0-dim entries ("Cannot pad
scalars"). Give such entries one dimension, or stack them separately.

### Strings and other Python objects

A list of strings, one for each element of the batch, becomes a
[`NonTensorStack`](../reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack). The strings can have any length:

```
>>> TensorDict({"text": ["a", "bb", "ccc"]}, batch_size=[3])[1]["text"]
'bb'
```

[Non-tensor data and unbatched entries](non_tensor.html#non-tensor-data) explains non-tensor data and what reads return.

### Choose an option

- To keep each element as it is, and to write into the elements, use a lazy
stack.
- To give a model one tensor with a mask, use `pad_sequence`, or
`get(key, as_padded_tensor=True)` on a lazy stack.
- To give a model a nested tensor, use `get(key, as_nested_tensor=True)` or
`densify(layout=torch.jagged)`.
- For strings and other Python objects, use a `NonTensorStack`.

## Lazy pre-allocation

To fill a tensordict one element at a time, create an empty tensordict with
the full batch size, and assign each element to an index. The first assignment
creates each entry, filled with zeros, with the batch size of the tensordict.
The next assignments write into these entries in place. In this example, a
simulation writes one state for each of its `N` steps:

```
>>> N = 4
>>> def simulate(i):
... return TensorDict({"pos": torch.full((3,), float(i)), "info": {"step": torch.tensor(i)}})
>>> data = TensorDict(batch_size=[N])
>>> for i in range(N):
... data[i] = simulate(i)
>>> data["pos"]
tensor([[0., 0., 0.],
 [1., 1., 1.],
 [2., 2., 2.],
 [3., 3., 3.]])
>>> data["info", "step"]
tensor([0, 1, 2, 3])
```

A later assignment can add a new key: the other elements of that entry are
zeros. A value with another shape raises a `RuntimeError`. The
[Filling a TensorDict row by row](../tutorials/tensordict_preallocation.html) tutorial steps through this loop.

[`lazy_stack()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.lazy_stack.html#tensordict.lazy_stack), [`maybe_dense_stack()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.maybe_dense_stack.html#tensordict.maybe_dense_stack),
[`cat()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.cat.html#tensordict.cat), and [`pad_sequence()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.pad_sequence.html#tensordict.pad_sequence) in the
[API reference](../reference/index.html#api-reference).
- The tutorials [Changing the shape of a TensorDict](../tutorials/tensordict_shapes.html) (stacking and
concatenating) and [Building tensordicts from streams](../tutorials/streamed_tensordict.html) (building lazy
stacks from a stream of data).

# Load data and share it between processes

A tensordict with a batch dimension is a dataset. A
[`DataLoader`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/data.html#torch.utils.data.DataLoader) reads each batch from it with one index
operation, and the batch is a tensordict. Processes on one node can also share
one tensordict, in shared memory or in memory-mapped files, and see the writes
of the other processes.

## Use a tensordict as a dataset

A tensordict is a map-style dataset: `len(td)` is the size of its first
batch dimension, and `td[i]` is one sample (see [Batch size, shapes, and indexing](concepts/batch_size.html#batch-size)). It also
has `__getitems__`, which reads a whole batch with one index operation.
Pass `collate_fn=lambda x: x` to keep that batch as it is:

```
>>> import torch
>>> from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict
>>> _ = torch.manual_seed(0)
>>> data = TensorDict(
... {"image": torch.randn(10, 1, 8, 8), "label": torch.arange(10)}, batch_size=[10]
... )
>>> loader = DataLoader(data, batch_size=4, shuffle=True, collate_fn=lambda x: x)
>>> batches = list(loader)
>>> [batch["label"].tolist() for batch in batches]
[[5, 1, 2, 7], [9, 4, 6, 3], [0, 8]]
>>> type(batches[0]).__name__, batches[0].batch_size
('TensorDict', torch.Size([4]))
```

The default `collate_fn` cannot read a tensordict. It raises
`TypeError: iteration over a 0-d tensordict`:

```
>>> next(iter(DataLoader(data, batch_size=4)))
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
TypeError: iteration over a 0-d tensordict. Use keys(), values() or items() to iterate over its entries.
```

The same works for a memory-mapped tensordict (see [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving)). Each batch
then reads only its rows from disk.

Without a `DataLoader`, index the tensordict with a permutation. With no
worker processes, this gives the same batches:

```
>>> for idx in torch.randperm(len(data)).split(4):
... batch = data[idx]
>>> batch.batch_size
torch.Size([2])
```

## A dataset that returns tensordicts

A dataset can return one tensordict for each sample, for example a list of
tensordicts, or a [`Dataset`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/data.html#torch.utils.data.Dataset) whose `__getitem__`
builds a tensordict. The `DataLoader` then gets a list of tensordicts for
each batch, and the default `collate_fn` raises the same `TypeError`.
Pass `collate_fn=torch.stack` to stack the list into one tensordict:

```
>>> samples = [TensorDict({"features": torch.randn(3), "label": i}) for i in range(10)]
>>> batch = next(iter(DataLoader(samples, batch_size=4, collate_fn=torch.stack)))
>>> batch.batch_size, batch["label"]
(torch.Size([4]), tensor([0, 1, 2, 3]))
```

If the samples have different shapes, `torch.stack` raises an error. Pass
[`lazy_stack()`](reference/generated/tensordict.lazy_stack.html#tensordict.lazy_stack) instead. It returns a
[`LazyStackedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict.html#tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict), which keeps each sample as it is
(see [Stacking and variable-size data](concepts/stacking.html#stacking)). This example loads point clouds with different numbers
of points:

```
>>> from tensordict import lazy_stack
>>> clouds = [TensorDict({"points": torch.randn(n, 3)}) for n in (5, 2, 7, 3)]
>>> batch = next(iter(DataLoader(clouds, batch_size=4, collate_fn=lazy_stack)))
>>> type(batch).__name__, batch.batch_size
('LazyStackedTensorDict', torch.Size([4]))
>>> [cloud["points"].shape for cloud in batch.unbind(0)]
[torch.Size([5, 3]), torch.Size([2, 3]), torch.Size([7, 3]), torch.Size([3, 3])]
```

[`collate()`](reference/generated/tensordict.collate.html#tensordict.collate) does both: it stacks the samples densely if
their shapes match, and lazily otherwise. It also reads samples that hold
tensordicts or tensorclasses in a tuple or a dict, such as `(td, label)`
pairs, which `torch.stack` cannot stack:

```
>>> from tensordict import collate
>>> pairs = [(TensorDict({"features": torch.randn(3)}), i) for i in range(10)]
>>> features, labels = next(iter(DataLoader(pairs, batch_size=4, collate_fn=collate)))
>>> type(features).__name__, features.batch_size, labels
('TensorDict', torch.Size([4]), tensor([0, 1, 2, 3]))
>>> batch = next(iter(DataLoader(clouds, batch_size=4, collate_fn=collate)))
>>> type(batch).__name__
'LazyStackedTensorDict'
```

## Batch samplers

A batch sampler gives the indices of a whole batch. Pass it as `sampler`,
with `batch_size=None`. The `DataLoader` then calls `data[indices]` with
the list of indices of each batch, and `collate_fn` gets the tensordict:

```
>>> from torch.utils.data import BatchSampler, SequentialSampler
>>> sampler = BatchSampler(SequentialSampler(data), batch_size=4, drop_last=True)
>>> loader = DataLoader(data, sampler=sampler, batch_size=None, collate_fn=lambda x: x)
>>> [batch["label"].tolist() for batch in loader]
[[0, 1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6, 7]]
```

## Worker processes and pinned memory

With `num_workers` greater than 0, the `DataLoader` reads the batches in
worker processes. Each worker gets the dataset when it starts:

- With the `fork` start method (the default on Linux up to Python 3.13),
the worker inherits a copy-on-write view of the memory of the main process.
- With `spawn` (the default on macOS and Windows) and `forkserver` (the
default on Linux from Python 3.14), the `DataLoader` pickles the dataset
to each worker. A memory-mapped tensordict pickles as its file names, so
the workers open the same files and do not copy the data. Pickle cannot
send a `lambda`, so define `collate_fn` as a function at the top level
of a module.

The worker examples start processes, so they are complete scripts. Save one
to a file and run it with `python`:

```
import tempfile

import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

from tensordict import TensorDict

def keep_batch(batch):
 return batch

if __name__ == "__main__":
 with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as path:
 data = TensorDict(
 {
 "image": torch.randn(1_000, 1, 8, 8),
 "label": torch.arange(1_000),
 },
 batch_size=[1_000],
 ).memmap_(path)
 loader = DataLoader(
 data, batch_size=100, shuffle=True, num_workers=2, collate_fn=keep_batch
 )
 total = sum(batch["label"].sum().item() for batch in loader)
 print(total) # 499500
```

With `pin_memory=True`, the `DataLoader` calls
[`pin_memory()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.pin_memory.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.pin_memory) on each batch, which pins every
leaf. From pinned memory, `to(device, non_blocking=True)` copies the batch
to the GPU while the CPU goes on. These lines need a GPU, so they are not run
when this page is tested:

```
>>> loader = DataLoader(data, batch_size=4, collate_fn=lambda x: x, pin_memory=True) 
>>> batch = next(iter(loader)).to("cuda", non_blocking=True)
```

Without a `DataLoader`, `td.to("cuda", non_blocking_pin=True)` pins the
leaves with several threads (`num_threads`), and copies them to the GPU
(see [Devices, dtypes, and memory](concepts/devices.html#devices)).

## Share a tensordict between processes

[`share_memory_()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.share_memory_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.share_memory_) moves each tensor of a
tensordict to shared memory. When you then pass the tensordict to another
process, as an argument or through a `torch.multiprocessing` queue, that
process uses the same memory. Each process sees the writes of the others,
without a copy.

`share_memory_` locks the tensordict, so write into its tensors in place,
for example with `td[i] = ...` or `td["x"].add_(1)` (see
[Locking and temporary changes](concepts/keys.html#keys-locking)). In this script, four processes each simulate one
system, and write its state into one row:

```
import torch
import torch.multiprocessing as mp

from tensordict import TensorDict

def simulate(systems, i):
 systems[i] = TensorDict({"state": torch.full((3,), float(i))})

if __name__ == "__main__":
 systems = TensorDict({"state": torch.zeros(4, 3)}, batch_size=[4]).share_memory_()
 processes = [mp.Process(target=simulate, args=(systems, i)) for i in range(4)]
 for p in processes:
 p.start()
 for p in processes:
 p.join()
 print(systems["state"][:, 0]) # tensor([0., 1., 2., 3.])
```

Call `share_memory_` before you start the processes. Without it, the
result depends on the start method. With `fork`, the child writes into a
copy, and the parent does not see the writes. With `spawn`, PyTorch moves
the tensors to shared memory when it pickles them, so the parent sees the
writes.

`memmap_()` works in the same way as `share_memory_()`, with the tensors
in files: memory-mapped files in a directory if you give a path, and
anonymous temporary files if you do not. Use files if the data is larger than
RAM, or if processes that you start later must open the data. The size of
`/dev/shm` limits shared memory.

A queue works the same way. The process that gets the tensordict uses the
memory of the process that sent it:

```
import torch
import torch.multiprocessing as mp

from tensordict import TensorDict

def consume(queue):
 systems = queue.get()
 systems["state"].add_(100)

if __name__ == "__main__":
 queue = mp.Queue()
 systems = TensorDict({"state": torch.zeros(4, 3)}, batch_size=[4]).share_memory_()
 p = mp.Process(target=consume, args=(queue,))
 p.start()
 queue.put(systems)
 p.join()
 print(systems["state"][0]) # tensor([100., 100., 100.])
```

## Several processes on one dataset on disk

Processes can also open a memory-mapped dataset by its path, with
[`load_memmap()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap). Readers that do not change the
data can pass `mode="r"` (see [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving)). tensordict does not lock the
files, so give each writer its own rows (see [Share data between processes](storage.html#storage-sharing)). This
script preallocates a dataset on disk, fills it from two processes, and reads
it back:

```
import tempfile

import torch
import torch.multiprocessing as mp

from tensordict import TensorDict

def fill(path, start, stop):
 data = TensorDict.load_memmap(path)
 for i in range(start, stop):
 data[i] = TensorDict({"image": torch.full((3, 8, 8), i, dtype=torch.uint8)})

if __name__ == "__main__":
 with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as path:
 TensorDict.from_schema(
 {"image": ([3, 8, 8], torch.uint8)},
 batch_size=[100],
 storage="memmap",
 prefix=path,
 )
 writers = [
 mp.Process(target=fill, args=(path, 0, 50)),
 mp.Process(target=fill, args=(path, 50, 100)),
 ]
 for p in writers:
 p.start()
 for p in writers:
 p.join()
 data = TensorDict.load_memmap(path, mode="r")
 # tensor([ 0, 49, 50, 99], dtype=torch.uint8)
 print(data["image"][[0, 49, 50, 99], 0, 0, 0])
```

## Process a dataset in parallel with map

[`map()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.map.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.map) splits a tensordict into chunks along
one dimension, calls a function on each chunk in a pool of processes, and
concatenates the results. If the tensordict is memory-mapped or in shared
memory, the chunks go to the workers without a copy. Return a new
tensordict from the function, and do not add keys to its input: the chunk of
a memory-mapped tensordict is locked. If you pass a preallocated
memory-mapped tensordict as `out`, the workers write the results into it.
This script computes the kinetic energy of 8 particles in two processes:

```
import tempfile

import torch

from tensordict import TensorDict

def kinetic_energy(chunk):
 energy = 0.5 * chunk["mass"] * (chunk["vel"] ** 2).sum(-1)
 return TensorDict({"energy": energy}, batch_size=chunk.batch_size)

if __name__ == "__main__":
 with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as path:
 particles = TensorDict(
 {
 "mass": torch.ones(8),
 "vel": torch.arange(8.0).unsqueeze(-1).repeat(1, 3),
 },
 batch_size=[8],
 ).memmap_()
 out = TensorDict({"energy": torch.zeros(8)}, batch_size=[8]).memmap_like(path)
 particles.map(kinetic_energy, num_workers=2, chunksize=2, out=out)
 # MemoryMappedTensor([ 0.0000, 1.5000, 6.0000, 13.5000])
 print(out["energy"][:4])
```

`map` also takes `num_chunks`, a `pool` that you create, and a
`generator` that seeds each worker. [`map_iter()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.map_iter.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.map_iter)
returns the results one chunk at a time.

# Distributed tensordicts

A tensordict sends, receives, and reduces all its tensors with one call:
`td.send(dst=1)` sends every leaf to rank 1, and `td.all_reduce()`
reduces every leaf over all ranks of [`torch.distributed`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.html#module-torch.distributed). To stream
tensordicts between two nodes without a process group, use a UCXX pipe. To
share a tensordict between processes on one node, see [Load data and share it between processes](data_loading.html#data-loading).

## Choose a method

These are methods of [`TensorDictBase`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase), so they also work
on tensorclasses.

| Method | Ranks that call it | Use it to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`send()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.send.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.send), [`recv()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.recv.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.recv) | sender and receiver | Send a tensordict to a rank that has a tensordict of the same structure. `consolidated=True` sends one message. |
| [`isend()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.isend.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.isend), [`irecv()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.irecv.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.irecv) | sender and receiver | Send as `send` does, and do other work while the data moves. |
| [`init_remote()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.init_remote.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.init_remote), [`from_remote_init()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_remote_init.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_remote_init) | sender and receiver (or all, with `use_broadcast=True`) | Send a tensordict to a rank that does not know its structure. |
| [`broadcast()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.broadcast.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.broadcast) | all | Send one tensordict from one rank to all ranks. |
| [`scatter()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.scatter.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.scatter) | all | Send a different tensordict from one rank to each rank. |
| [`all_gather()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.all_gather.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.all_gather) | all | Get the tensordicts of all ranks on every rank. |
| [`gather_and_stack()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.gather_and_stack.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.gather_and_stack) | all | Stack the tensordicts of the other ranks on one rank. |
| [`all_reduce()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.all_reduce.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.all_reduce) | all | Reduce each leaf over all ranks, in place on every rank (for example, to average gradients). |
| [`reduce()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.reduce.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.reduce) | all | Reduce each leaf over all ranks, on one rank. |

## Run the examples

Every process must join a process group before it calls these methods (see
[`torch.distributed.init_process_group()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.html#torch.distributed.init_process_group)). The script below starts two
processes on one machine, with the `gloo` backend on CPU, and runs one
example in each. Each example on this page is a function of `rank` and
`world_size`. To run an example, add it to the script, and pass its name to
`run` in the last line:

```
import os
import shutil
import socket
import tempfile

import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.multiprocessing as mp

from tensordict import TensorDict

def _worker(rank, world_size, port, example):
 os.environ["MASTER_ADDR"] = "127.0.0.1"
 os.environ["MASTER_PORT"] = str(port)
 dist.init_process_group("gloo", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)
 try:
 example(rank, world_size)
 finally:
 dist.destroy_process_group()

def run(example, world_size=2):
 with socket.socket() as s: # find a free port
 s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
 port = s.getsockname()[1]
 mp.spawn(_worker, args=(world_size, port, example), nprocs=world_size)

def send_recv(rank, world_size):
 if rank == 0:
 td = TensorDict({"a": torch.randn(4), "b": torch.randn(4, 3)}, batch_size=[4])
 td.send(dst=1)
 elif rank == 1:
 td = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(4), "b": torch.zeros(4, 3)}, batch_size=[4])
 td.recv(src=0)
 print((td["b"] != 0).all()) # tensor(True)

if __name__ == "__main__":
 run(send_recv)
```

On several machines, or with GPUs, start one process for each GPU with
`torchrun`. Call `dist.init_process_group("nccl")` and
`torch.cuda.set_device(rank)`, and put the tensordicts on the GPU. The
calls on this page do not change.

## Send to one rank

### send and recv

The `send_recv` example above sends each leaf as one message. The receiver
must hold a tensordict with the same keys, shapes, and dtypes. `recv` writes
the received values into its tensors.

With `consolidated=True`, `send` sends all the leaves as one message
instead. It first calls [`consolidate()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate), which
copies the leaves into one storage (see [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving)), unless the tensordict
is consolidated already. This is faster when the tensordict has many small
leaves. In one measurement with 100 leaves of 256 bytes, on one machine with
`gloo`, a consolidated send was 34 times as fast as a send per leaf. The receiver must
hold a consolidated tensordict with the same keys, shapes, and dtypes:

```
def send_consolidated(rank, world_size):
 if rank == 0:
 td = TensorDict({"a": torch.randn(4), "b": torch.randn(4, 3)}, batch_size=[4])
 td.send(dst=1, consolidated=True)
 elif rank == 1:
 td = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(4), "b": torch.zeros(4, 3)}, batch_size=[4])
 td = td.consolidate(metadata=True)
 td.recv(src=0, consolidated=True)
 print((td["b"] != 0).all()) # tensor(True)
```

If the receiver is not consolidated, `recv(consolidated=True)` raises
`AttributeError: 'TensorDict' object has no attribute '_consolidated'`, and
the sender waits until its timeout.

### isend and irecv

[`isend()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.isend.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.isend) and
[`irecv()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.irecv.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.irecv) start one transfer for each leaf. By
default, both wait until all the transfers are done, as `send` and
`recv` do. To do other work while the data moves, pass
`return_early=True` to `isend`, or `return_premature=True` to
`irecv`. The call then returns a list of `Work` objects. Call `wait()`
on each one before you use or change the data:

```
def isend_irecv(rank, world_size):
 if rank == 0:
 td = TensorDict({"a": torch.randn(4), "b": torch.randn(4, 3)}, batch_size=[4])
 works = td.isend(dst=1, return_early=True)
 # ... do other work, without changing td ...
 for work in works:
 work.wait()
 elif rank == 1:
 td = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(4), "b": torch.zeros(4, 3)}, batch_size=[4])
 works = td.irecv(src=0, return_premature=True)
 # ... do other work, without reading td ...
 for work in works:
 work.wait()
 print((td["b"] != 0).all()) # tensor(True)
```

### A receiver that does not know the structure

If the receiver does not know the keys, shapes, and dtypes of the tensordict,
call [`init_remote()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.init_remote.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.init_remote) on the sender and
[`from_remote_init()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_remote_init.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_remote_init) on the receiver. The
sender sends the metadata, then the data. The receiver builds a new
tensordict, which is consolidated. A tensorclass arrives as the same
tensorclass, if the receiver can import its class.

After this first transfer, send the next batches with
`send(consolidated=True)` and `recv(consolidated=True)`, into the
tensordict that `from_remote_init` returned. The receiver then does not
allocate memory again:

```
def cold_start(rank, world_size):
 if rank == 0:
 td = TensorDict(
 {"obs": torch.randn(2, 84), "reward": torch.randn(2, 1)}, batch_size=[2]
 )
 td.init_remote(dst=1)
 for step in range(3):
 td["obs"].add_(1)
 td.send(dst=1, consolidated=True)
 elif rank == 1:
 td = TensorDict.from_remote_init(src=0)
 print(td.batch_size, td.is_consolidated()) # torch.Size([2]) True
 for step in range(3):
 td.recv(src=0, consolidated=True)
```

With `use_broadcast=True`, `init_remote` and `from_remote_init` call
[`broadcast()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.broadcast.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.broadcast) instead, and all the ranks of
the group must call them:

```
def cold_start_broadcast(rank, world_size):
 if rank == 0:
 td = TensorDict({"obs": torch.randn(2, 84)}, batch_size=[2])
 td.init_remote(use_broadcast=True)
 else:
 td = TensorDict.from_remote_init(src=0, use_broadcast=True)
 print(td["obs"].shape) # torch.Size([2, 84])
```

## Collectives

Every rank of the group must call a collective. The methods that send the
structure (`broadcast`, `scatter`, `all_gather`,
`gather_and_stack`, `init_remote`) send it with the object collectives of
[`torch.distributed`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.html#module-torch.distributed), which use pickle.

Warning

Use these methods only in a process group whose ranks you trust. Each
receiver unpickles the metadata that the sender sends.

### broadcast

[`broadcast()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.broadcast.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.broadcast) sends the tensordict of rank
`src` to all ranks, and returns it on each rank, consolidated. The other
ranks can start with an empty tensordict:

```
def broadcast(rank, world_size):
 td = TensorDict({"a": torch.arange(3.0)}, batch_size=[3]) if rank == 0 else TensorDict()
 td = td.broadcast(src=0)
 print(rank, td["a"]) # tensor([0., 1., 2.]) on every rank
```

### all_reduce and reduce

[`all_reduce()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.all_reduce.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.all_reduce) reduces each leaf over all
ranks, in place. With `async_op=True`, it returns a list of `Work`
objects to wait on:

```
def all_reduce(rank, world_size):
 td = TensorDict({"a": torch.ones(3) * rank}, batch_size=[3])
 td.all_reduce(op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)
 print(rank, td["a"]) # with 2 ranks: tensor([1., 1., 1.]) on every rank
 works = td.all_reduce(async_op=True)
 for work in works:
 work.wait()
```

[`reduce()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.reduce.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.reduce) writes the result on rank `dst`
only. On the other ranks, the values of the tensordict after the call are
not defined: with `gloo` and 3 ranks, rank 1 held partial sums. If you need
the local values after the call, clone the tensordict before it:

```
def reduce(rank, world_size):
 td = TensorDict({"a": torch.ones(3) * (rank + 1)}, batch_size=[3])
 td.reduce(dst=0, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)
 if rank == 0:
 print(td["a"]) # with 2 ranks: tensor([3., 3., 3.])
```

### all_gather, scatter, and gather_and_stack

[`all_gather()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.all_gather.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.all_gather) returns a list with the
tensordict of each rank, on every rank. The tensordicts can have different
structures:

```
def all_gather(rank, world_size):
 local = TensorDict({"a": torch.full((3,), float(rank))}, batch_size=[3])
 tds = local.all_gather()
 print(rank, [td["a"][0].item() for td in tds]) # [0.0, 1.0] on every rank
```

[`scatter()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.scatter.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.scatter) sends one tensordict of a list
on rank `src` to each rank. The other ranks pass `tensordicts=None`:

```
def scatter(rank, world_size):
 if rank == 0:
 tds = [
 TensorDict({"a": torch.full((3,), float(i))}, batch_size=[3])
 for i in range(world_size)
 ]
 else:
 tds = None
 td = TensorDict().scatter(src=0, tensordicts=tds)
 # tensor([0., 0., 0.]) on rank 0, tensor([1., 1., 1.]) on rank 1
 print(rank, td["a"])
```

[`gather_and_stack()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.gather_and_stack.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.gather_and_stack) stacks the tensordicts of
the other ranks into the tensordict of rank `dst`, in place. The
tensordict of rank `dst` must have one row for each other rank: its first
dimension is `world_size - 1`. Its own data is not in the result:

```
def gather_and_stack(rank, world_size):
 if rank == 0:
 out = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(world_size - 1, 3)}, batch_size=[world_size - 1])
 out.gather_and_stack(dst=0)
 print(out["a"][:, 0]) # with 2 ranks: tensor([1.])
 else:
 td = TensorDict({"a": torch.full((3,), float(rank))}, batch_size=[3])
 td.gather_and_stack(dst=0)
```

## Several transfers and custom groups

`send`, `recv`, `isend`, and `irecv` mark the message of each leaf with
a tag: `init_tag`, `init_tag + 1`, and so on. If two tensordicts go
from one rank to another at the same time, give them tag ranges that do not
overlap. Pass the same `init_tag` on both sides. With
`pseudo_rand=True`, the tags are pseudo-random numbers instead. Generating
them costs about 10 µs for each leaf.

```
def two_transfers(rank, world_size):
 if rank == 0:
 obs = TensorDict({"a": torch.ones(4), "b": torch.ones(4)}, batch_size=[4])
 reward = TensorDict({"r": torch.full((4,), 2.0)}, batch_size=[4])
 works = obs.isend(dst=1, init_tag=0, return_early=True)
 works += reward.isend(dst=1, init_tag=100, return_early=True)
 for work in works:
 work.wait()
 elif rank == 1:
 obs = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(4), "b": torch.zeros(4)}, batch_size=[4])
 reward = TensorDict({"r": torch.zeros(4)}, batch_size=[4])
 reward.irecv(src=0, init_tag=100)
 obs.irecv(src=0, init_tag=0)
 print(obs["a"][0], reward["r"][0]) # tensor(1.) tensor(2.)
```

Each method takes a `group`. For `send` and `recv`, `dst` and `src`
are global ranks. To give a rank relative to the group, pass `group_dst` or
`group_src` instead. With them, a standalone `ProcessGroup` that you
built against a store also works. All ranks must call
[`torch.distributed.new_group()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.html#torch.distributed.new_group), also the ranks that are not in the
group:

```
def custom_group(rank, world_size):
 group = dist.new_group([0, world_size - 1])
 if rank == 0:
 TensorDict({"a": torch.ones(3)}, batch_size=[3]).send(group=group, group_dst=1)
 elif rank == world_size - 1:
 td = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3])
 td.recv(group=group, group_src=0)
 print(td["a"]) # tensor([1., 1., 1.])
```

## A dataset on a shared file system

If the nodes share a file system (for example NFS or Lustre), they can open
the same memory-mapped tensordict. No tensor then goes over the network:

1. On one rank, preallocate the files with
[`from_schema()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_schema.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_schema) (see [Large datasets and storage backends](storage.html#storage)). It
does not allocate the dataset in memory.
2. On each rank, write only its own rows. tensordict does not order the
writes between ranks (see [Share data between processes](storage.html#storage-sharing)).
3. Wait at a barrier before you read the rows of the other ranks. Ranks that
only read can load the files with `mode="r"` (see [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving)).

The script of Run the examples imports `shutil` and `tempfile` for
this example:

```
def shared_dataset(rank, world_size):
 # On a cluster, use a directory on the shared file system.
 path = [tempfile.mkdtemp() if rank == 0 else None]
 dist.broadcast_object_list(path, src=0)
 path = path[0]
 if rank == 0:
 TensorDict.from_schema(
 {"image": ([3, 64, 64], torch.uint8), "label": ([], torch.int64)},
 batch_size=[1_000],
 storage="memmap",
 prefix=path,
 )
 dist.barrier()
 data = TensorDict.load_memmap(path)
 rows = torch.arange(rank, 1_000, world_size)
 data["label"][rows] = rows
 dist.barrier()
 reader = TensorDict.load_memmap(path, mode="r")
 print(rank, reader["label"][:4]) # MemoryMappedTensor([0, 1, 2, 3]) on every rank
 dist.barrier()
 if rank == 0:
 shutil.rmtree(path)
```

## Stream between nodes with UCXX

Warning

`TensorDictPipe`, `TensorDictServer`, `send_tensordict`, and
`recv_tensordict` are experimental: their API can change in a minor
release without a deprecation cycle.

Warning

UCXX helpers, pipes, and servers require trusted peers and a trusted
network. The TensorDict protocol does not authenticate or authorize peers.
Peers control allocation sizes and, for pipes, the default receive device.
Set the receiver's `device=` to pin placement. Metadata checks do not
bound memory use or prevent out-of-memory errors from large valid messages.
After a protocol error, close the connection rather than retrying a receive.

[`TensorDictPipe`](reference/generated/tensordict._ucxx.TensorDictPipe.html#tensordict._ucxx.TensorDictPipe) sends tensordicts from one process
to one other process over [UCXX](https://github.com/rapidsai/ucxx), the
Python bindings of [UCX](https://openucx.org/). Use it when one node
streams batches to another, for example a data producer that feeds a
trainer. Compared with `send` and `recv` of `torch.distributed`:

- It needs no process group. The two sides connect by IP address and port.
- After the first message, the receiver writes each new batch into the same
buffer. It does not allocate memory or parse metadata.
- UCX selects the transport: TCP, InfiniBand verbs, or RoCE.
- If the tensors are on a GPU and GPUDirect RDMA is available, the buffer
goes from GPU memory to the network, with no copy in CPU memory.
- The API uses [`asyncio`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio.html#module-asyncio), and has synchronous wrappers.

The classes are in the private module `tensordict._ucxx`, and they need
the `ucxx` package. The examples of this section are not run when this page
is tested: `ucxx` is not installed on the machines that test it.

### Install UCXX

UCXX needs Linux, Python 3.11+, and the UCX system libraries. The `pip`
packages are built for CUDA:

```
pip install ucxx-cu12 # CUDA 12
pip install ucxx-cu13 # CUDA 13
conda install -c conda-forge -c rapidsai ucxx
```

For InfiniBand, the host needs `rdma-core` (or MOFED 5.0+) and Linux
5.6+. For GPUDirect RDMA, load the `nvidia_peermem` kernel module. To list
the InfiniBand devices and see whether the module is loaded:

```
ibstat
lsmod | grep nvidia_peermem
```

UCX selects the transports. To choose them, set environment variables before
the process imports `ucxx`:

```
export UCX_TLS=all # let UCX select (the default)
export UCX_NET_DEVICES=all
export UCX_TLS=tcp # TCP only, to debug
```

### How a pipe sends a tensordict

A pipe sends a consolidated tensordict (one storage and its metadata) in two
phases:

1. On the first message, the sender sends the metadata (keys, dtypes,
shapes, byte offsets, as JSON), then the storage. The receiver allocates
one buffer, and builds a tensordict whose leaves are views into it.
2. On the next messages with the same structure, the sender sends a one-byte
flag, then the storage only. The receiver writes it into the buffer of
the first message.

If the structure changes (other keys, shapes, or dtypes), the pipe sends the
metadata again. The sender compares a hash of the metadata at each send. If
the tensordict is not consolidated, the sender consolidates it at each send,
which allocates a new buffer. To avoid that, consolidate once and copy each
batch into the consolidated tensordict.

### Connect two processes

One side listens on a port, and the other connects to it. `pipe.arecv()`
returns the received tensordict. From the second message on, it returns the
same tensordict, with the new values:

```
import asyncio

import torch

from tensordict import TensorDict
from tensordict._ucxx import TensorDictPipe

async def receiver(): # on node A, with IP address 10.0.1.1
 pipe = await TensorDictPipe.listen(port=13337)
 for _ in range(100):
 td = await pipe.arecv() # the same tensordict after the first message
 train(td)
 await pipe.aclose()

async def sender(): # on node B
 pipe = await TensorDictPipe.connect("10.0.1.1", port=13337)
 buffer = None
 for obs, label in dataloader:
 batch = TensorDict({"obs": obs, "label": label}, batch_size=[obs.shape[0]])
 if buffer is None:
 buffer = batch.consolidate(metadata=True) # allocate once
 else:
 buffer.update_(batch) # copy into the consolidated storage
 await pipe.asend(buffer)
 await pipe.aclose()
```

`update_` needs batches with the same shapes. If the last batch is
smaller, consolidate it on its own.

A pipe is also an async context manager, and an async iterator:

```
async with await TensorDictPipe.listen(13337) as pipe:
 async for td in pipe:
 train(td)
```

The `async for` loop ends when the pipe is closed. It also ends when an
error happens: the iterator turns every exception into the end of the loop,
and does not raise it. If you need the error, call `await pipe.arecv()` in
a `while` loop instead.

`pipe.send(td)`, `pipe.recv()`, and `pipe.close()` are synchronous
wrappers. If no event loop runs in the thread, each call runs the coroutine
with [`asyncio.run()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-runner.html#asyncio.run). In a coroutine, or in a callback of a running event
loop, use the async methods (`asend`, `arecv`, `aclose`). There, a
synchronous wrapper raises a `RuntimeError` that names the async method to
await, for example "TensorDictPipe.arecv() cannot run synchronously inside a
running event loop".
`TensorDictPipe.listen` and `TensorDictPipe.connect` are coroutines only.

### GPU tensors

If the leaves of the sender are on a GPU, the consolidated buffer is on the
GPU, and the pipe sends it from GPU memory. The receiver allocates its buffer
on the device of the sender, unless you pass `device`:

```
td = TensorDict({"x": torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="cuda")}, batch_size=[1024])
await pipe.asend(td) # sender

td = await pipe.arecv() # receiver: td is on cuda
td = await pipe.arecv(device="cpu") # or receive on the CPU
```

### send and recv with a pipe

[`send()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.send.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.send) and
[`recv()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.recv.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.recv) also take a `TensorDictPipe` instead
of a rank, and [`asend()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.asend.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.asend) and
[`arecv()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.arecv.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.arecv) are their async versions. With a
pipe, `recv` does not always write into `td`. It writes into `td` and
returns `td` if `td` is consolidated and has the layout of the sent
tensordict. Otherwise it leaves `td` unchanged and returns a tensordict of
the pipe: a new consolidated tensordict when the message brings a new schema,
and the tensordict that received the previous message when the schema has not
changed. A pipe made with `consolidated=False` never writes into `td`.
Keep the return value, and receive into it:

```
td.send(dst=pipe) # sender

td = td.recv(src=pipe) # receiver: use the return value
td = await td.arecv(pipe) # the async version
```

### Several clients: TensorDictServer

[`TensorDictServer`](reference/generated/tensordict._ucxx.TensorDictServer.html#tensordict._ucxx.TensorDictServer) accepts several connections, and
gives a `TensorDictPipe` for each client. Each pipe can send and receive:

```
from tensordict._ucxx import TensorDictServer

async def handle_client(pipe):
 async for td in pipe:
 await pipe.asend(model(td))

async with TensorDictServer(port=13337) as server:
 await server.serve(handle_client)
```

To handle each connection yourself, iterate over the server:

```
async with TensorDictServer(port=13337) as server:
 async for pipe in server:
 asyncio.ensure_future(handle_client(pipe))
```

### Benchmarks

These numbers come from the pull request that added UCXX
([#1611](https://github.com/pytorch/tensordict/pull/1611), March 2026). It
measured them on two nodes with NVIDIA H200 GPUs and 400 Gb/s InfiniBand,
with `nvidia_peermem` loaded. This page does not repeat the measurement.
The script is `benchmarks/distributed/bench_transport.py`. It needs a Ray
cluster of two nodes, or the `RANK`, `MASTER_ADDR`, and `PEER_ADDR`
environment variables.

Each tensordict has two leaves of the size in the "Size" column, so each
message has twice that size. Each time is the mean of 10 rounds, after 2
warm-up rounds. The UCXX rows are the steady state, after the first
message.

| Size | Method | Latency | Throughput |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 KB | gloo `send`/`recv`, one message per leaf | 900 µs | |
| 1 KB | gloo `send`/`recv`, consolidated | 212 µs | |
| 1 KB | UCXX pipe | 105 µs | |
| 1 MB | gloo `send`/`recv`, one message per leaf | 963 µs | 2.18 GB/s |
| 1 MB | gloo `send`/`recv`, consolidated | 903 µs | 2.32 GB/s |
| 1 MB | UCXX pipe | 682 µs | 3.08 GB/s |
| 100 MB | gloo `send`/`recv`, one message per leaf | 87 ms | 2.40 GB/s |
| 100 MB | gloo `send`/`recv`, consolidated | 87 ms | 2.42 GB/s |
| 100 MB | gloo `broadcast` | 159 ms | 1.32 GB/s |
| 100 MB | UCXX pipe | 37 ms | 5.71 GB/s |

At 100 MB, the UCXX pipe took 37 ms and the fastest gloo method 87 ms.

| Size | Method | Latency | Throughput |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 KB | NCCL `send`/`recv`, one message per leaf | 231 µs | |
| 1 KB | UCXX pipe | 138 µs | |
| 1 MB | NCCL `send`/`recv`, one message per leaf | 238 µs | 8.81 GB/s |
| 1 MB | UCXX pipe | 231 µs | 9.08 GB/s |
| 100 MB | NCCL `send`/`recv`, one message per leaf | 7.50 ms | 27.95 GB/s |
| 100 MB | UCXX pipe | 7.47 ms | 28.08 GB/s |

On the GPU, NCCL and the UCXX pipe had the same throughput at 1 MB and
100 MB. At 1 KB, the UCXX pipe had a lower latency (138 µs and 231 µs). Both
used GPUDirect RDMA: the storage went from the GPU to the network without a
copy to the CPU.

- [Large datasets and storage backends](storage.html#storage): memory-mapped datasets, and Redis stores that processes on
several nodes share.
- [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving): consolidated tensordicts.

# FX tracing (prototype)

`tensordict.prototype.fx.symbolic_trace()` traces a
[`TensorDictModule`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule) or a
[`TensorDictSequential`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential) into a [`torch.fx`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/fx.html#module-torch.fx) graph
that you can read and transform. Use it instead of
[`torch.fx.symbolic_trace()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/fx.html#torch.fx.symbolic_trace), which raises `TypeError: 'TensorDictModule'
object is not subscriptable` on a [`TensorDictModule`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule).

Warning

`tensordict.prototype.fx` is a prototype. Its API can change without a
deprecation cycle. To make a module faster or to export it, use
[`torch.compile()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.compile.html#torch.compile) or [`torch.export.export()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/user_guide/torch_compiler/export/api_reference.html#torch.export.export) (see
[torch.compile, torch.func, torch.export, and CUDA graphs](compile.html#compile)). If you find a problem, open an issue.

## Trace a `TensorDictModule`

This example creates a [`TensorDictModule`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule) (see
[Modules: TensorDictModule and tensordict.nn](modules.html#modules-guide)), traces it, and prints the graph and the generated
code.

Tracing a TensorDictModule

```
>>> import torch
>>> import torch.nn as nn
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict
>>> from tensordict.nn import TensorDictModule
>>> from tensordict.prototype.fx import symbolic_trace

>>> class Net(nn.Module):
... def __init__(self):
... super().__init__()
... self.linear = nn.LazyLinear(1)
...
... def forward(self, x):
... logits = self.linear(x)
... return logits, torch.sigmoid(logits)
>>> module = TensorDictModule(
... Net(),
... in_keys=["input"],
... out_keys=[("outputs", "logits"), ("outputs", "probabilities")],
... )
>>> graph_module = symbolic_trace(module)
>>> print(graph_module.graph)
graph():
 %tensordict : [num_users=1] = placeholder[target=tensordict]
 %getitem : [num_users=1] = call_function[target=operator.getitem](args = (%tensordict, input), kwargs = {})
 %linear : [num_users=2] = call_module[target=linear](args = (%getitem,), kwargs = {})
 %sigmoid : [num_users=1] = call_function[target=torch.sigmoid](args = (%linear,), kwargs = {})
 return (linear, sigmoid)
>>> print(graph_module.code)
def forward(self, tensordict):
 getitem = tensordict['input']; tensordict = None
 linear = self.linear(getitem); getitem = None
 sigmoid = torch.sigmoid(linear)
 return (linear, sigmoid)
```

A forward pass with each module gives the same outputs:

```
>>> tensordict = TensorDict({"input": torch.randn(32, 100)}, [32])
>>> module_out = module(tensordict, tensordict_out=TensorDict())
>>> graph_module_out = graph_module(tensordict, tensordict_out=TensorDict())
>>> assert (
... module_out["outputs", "logits"] == graph_module_out["outputs", "logits"]
... ).all()
>>> assert (
... module_out["outputs", "probabilities"]
... == graph_module_out["outputs", "probabilities"]
... ).all()
```

## Trace a `TensorDictSequential`

`symbolic_trace()` also traces a
[`TensorDictSequential`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential). The whole sequence becomes one
graph: each module gets its inputs from the outputs of the modules before it
in the graph, not from the input [`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict). This
example traces a sequence of two modules:

Tracing TensorDictSequential

```
>>> import torch
>>> import torch.nn as nn
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict
>>> from tensordict.nn import TensorDictModule, TensorDictSequential
>>> from tensordict.prototype.fx import symbolic_trace

>>> class Net(nn.Module):
... def __init__(self, input_size=100, hidden_size=50, output_size=10):
... super().__init__()
... self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size)
... self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, output_size)
...
... def forward(self, x):
... x = torch.relu(self.fc1(x))
... return self.fc2(x)
>>> class Masker(nn.Module):
... def forward(self, x, mask):
... return torch.softmax(x * mask, dim=1)
>>> net = TensorDictModule(
... Net(), in_keys=[("input", "x")], out_keys=[("intermediate", "x")]
... )
>>> masker = TensorDictModule(
... Masker(),
... in_keys=[("intermediate", "x"), ("input", "mask")],
... out_keys=[("output", "probabilities")],
... )
>>> module = TensorDictSequential(net, masker)
>>> graph_module = symbolic_trace(module)
>>> print(graph_module.code)
def forward(self, tensordict):
 getitem = tensordict[('input', 'x')]
 _0_fc1 = getattr(self, "0").module.fc1(getitem); getitem = None
 relu = torch.relu(_0_fc1); _0_fc1 = None
 _0_fc2 = getattr(self, "0").module.fc2(relu); relu = None
 getitem_1 = tensordict[('input', 'mask')]; tensordict = None
 mul = _0_fc2 * getitem_1; getitem_1 = None
 softmax = torch.softmax(mul, dim = 1); mul = None
 return (_0_fc2, softmax)
```

To draw the graph, install the `pydot`
package and the Graphviz `dot` program:

Visualizing the graph

```
>>> import os
>>> import tempfile
>>> from torch.fx.passes.graph_drawer import FxGraphDrawer
>>> g = FxGraphDrawer(graph_module, "sequential")
>>> path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "graph.svg")
>>> with open(path, "wb") as f:
... _ = f.write(g.get_dot_graph().create_svg())
```

The result is this drawing:

![Visualization of the traced graph.](_images/graph.svg)

## Limitations

The traced module is a `TDGraphModule`. It differs from the module that it
traces:

- It ignores `selected_out_keys` of a
[`TensorDictSequential`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential). It writes every
`out_keys` entry of every module in the sequence, including the
intermediate ones, such as `("intermediate", "x")` above.
- It takes a tensordict only. A call with tensors as keyword arguments, such
as `graph_module(x=torch.randn(32, 100))`, raises `TypeError`.
- It writes its outputs into the input tensordict, unless you pass
`tensordict_out`.

## See also

- [torch.compile, torch.func, torch.export, and CUDA graphs](compile.html#compile): [`torch.compile()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.compile.html#torch.compile) and [`torch.export.export()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/user_guide/torch_compiler/export/api_reference.html#torch.export.export)
with tensordicts and tensordict modules.
- [Modules: TensorDictModule and tensordict.nn](modules.html#modules-guide): [`TensorDictModule`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule) and
[`TensorDictSequential`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential).
- The PyTorch documentation of [`torch.fx`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/fx.html#module-torch.fx).
