# TensorClass

A *tensorclass* is a class for tensor data. You declare its fields with type
annotations, as in a [`dataclass()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html#dataclasses.dataclass), and you write its methods
once. A method then runs on one item or on a batch of any shape, and compiles
with `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)`. The instances have the tensor
operations of a [`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict): indexing, reshaping,
`to(device)`, `torch.stack`, `torch.cat`, and saving to disk.

```
>>> import torch
>>> from tensordict import TensorClass
>>> class Particles(TensorClass):
... pos: torch.Tensor # [*batch, 3]
... vel: torch.Tensor # [*batch, 3]
... mass: torch.Tensor # [*batch]
...
... def step(self, force: torch.Tensor, dt: float) -> "Particles":
... vel = self.vel + dt * force / self.mass.unsqueeze(-1)
... return Particles(
... pos=self.pos + dt * vel, vel=vel, mass=self.mass, batch_size=self.batch_size
... )
>>> _ = torch.manual_seed(0)
>>> systems = Particles( # 64 systems of 1,000 particles each
... pos=torch.randn(64, 1000, 3),
... vel=torch.zeros(64, 1000, 3),
... mass=torch.ones(64, 1000),
... batch_size=[64, 1000],
... )
>>> systems = systems.step(torch.randn(64, 1000, 3), dt=0.01) # all 64 systems
>>> one = systems[0].step(torch.randn(1000, 3), dt=0.01) # one system
>>> type(one).__name__, one.batch_size
('Particles', torch.Size([1000]))
>>> grid = systems.reshape(8, 8, 1000).step(torch.randn(8, 8, 1000, 3), dt=0.01)
>>> grid.batch_size
torch.Size([8, 8, 1000])
>>> step = torch.compile(Particles.step, fullgraph=True)
>>> force = torch.randn(64, 1000, 3)
>>> torch.allclose(step(systems, force, 0.01).pos, systems.step(force, 0.01).pos)
True
```

`step` has no loop over the systems and no shape argument. The *batch size*
(`[64, 1000]` here) is the leading dimensions that all the fields share (see
[Batch size, shapes, and indexing](concepts/batch_size.html#batch-size)). An index or a `reshape` applies to these dimensions and
returns a `Particles`. So the same method runs on one system or on a grid
of systems. The compiled `step` gives the same result as the eager
`step`. The class declares its fields, so your editor completes
`self.pos`, and a type checker reads the fields as the signature of the
constructor (see Static type checking).

Read the quick start and Methods first. Each later section
describes one feature: read it when you need that feature. To compare a
tensorclass with a `TensorDict` and the other containers, see
[Which container should I use?](choosing_a_container.html#choosing-a-container).

## Quick start

Subclass [`TensorClass`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass) and annotate each field. Then pass
the values and the batch size to the constructor:

```
>>> from typing import Optional
>>> class Reading(TensorClass):
... signal: torch.Tensor
... count: torch.Tensor
... sensor: str
... backup: Optional["Reading"] = None
>>> data = Reading(
... signal=torch.randn(3, 4, 5),
... count=torch.randint(10, (3, 4, 1)),
... sensor="lidar",
... batch_size=[3, 4], # for example, 3 robots and 4 time steps
... )
>>> print(data)
Reading(
 count=Tensor(shape=torch.Size([3, 4, 1]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.int64, is_shared=False),
 sensor=NonTensorData(data=lidar, batch_size=torch.Size([3, 4]), device=None),
 signal=Tensor(shape=torch.Size([3, 4, 5]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False),
 backup=None,
 batch_size=torch.Size([3, 4]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
```

The `backup` annotation is a string because the class refers to itself.
Another way is `from __future__ import annotations` at the top of the
module. If you do not pass `batch_size`, it is `torch.Size([])`, and the
tensorclass has no batch dimensions.

Read and assign the fields as attributes. A field that is not a tensor
(`sensor` here) returns its plain value:

```
>>> data.sensor
'lidar'
>>> data.backup = Reading(
... signal=torch.randn(3, 4, 5),
... count=torch.randint(10, (3, 4, 1)),
... sensor="radar",
... batch_size=[3, 4],
... )
```

An index applies to the batch dimensions of every field, also in the nested
tensorclass. Fields that are not tensors keep their value:

```
>>> sub = data[:2]
>>> sub.batch_size
torch.Size([2, 4])
>>> sub.backup.signal.shape
torch.Size([2, 4, 5])
>>> sub.backup.sensor
'radar'
```

The shape and device operations of [`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict) work on a
tensorclass: `stack`, `cat`, `reshape`, `to`, `clone`, `apply`, and
the others. They return an instance of the same class:

```
>>> data2 = data.clone()
>>> cat_tc = torch.cat([data, data2], 0)
>>> type(cat_tc).__name__, cat_tc.batch_size
('Reading', torch.Size([6, 4]))
```

A tensorclass is not a [`TensorDictBase`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase) and not a
[`Mapping`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping). A string index raises an error, because an
index always applies to the batch dimensions. To read a field by name, use
`get`:

```
>>> data["count"]
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ValueError: Invalid indexing arguments: 'count'. A tensorclass is indexed along its batch dimensions; to read a field, use the attribute or get('count').
>>> data.get("count").shape
torch.Size([3, 4, 1])
```

Assigning a name that is not a field, as an attribute or with `set()`,
raises `AttributeError`. `set_non_tensor()`, `setdefault()`,
`create_nested()`, `rename_key_()`, `update()` with a `TensorDict`
or another tensorclass, and an indexed assignment of a `TensorDict`
(`data[idx] = td`) still store such a key, and warn with a
`DeprecationWarning`. Starting with TensorDict 0.17, they raise
`AttributeError` too.

To test whether an object is a tensordict or a tensorclass, use
[`is_tensor_collection()`](reference/generated/tensordict.is_tensor_collection.html#tensordict.is_tensor_collection). `to_tensordict()` returns a copy
of the data as a [`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict).

## Methods

A tensorclass is a Python class: you can add methods, properties, class
methods, and class constants to it. Of the dataclass features,
`__post_init__`, field defaults, and a custom `__init__` work, with the
rules below.

### Methods and properties

Methods and properties can read and assign the fields. A method that calls a
tensordict operation, such as `apply`, returns an instance of the class. A
property is not a field: it is not stored and not in `keys()`. Use
`typing.ClassVar` for a constant of the class. It is not a field
either:

```
>>> from typing import ClassVar
>>> class Logits(TensorClass):
... logits: torch.Tensor
... temperature: ClassVar[float] = 2.0
...
... @classmethod
... def uniform(cls, batch, n):
... return cls(logits=torch.zeros(batch, n), batch_size=[batch])
...
... @property
... def probs(self):
... return (self.logits / self.temperature).softmax(-1)
...
... @probs.setter
... def probs(self, value):
... self.logits = value.log() * self.temperature
...
... def detached(self):
... return self.apply(lambda t: t.detach())
>>> x = Logits.uniform(2, 4)
>>> x.probs[0]
tensor([0.2500, 0.2500, 0.2500, 0.2500])
>>> x.probs = torch.tensor([0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2]).expand(2, 4)
>>> x.probs[0]
tensor([0.4000, 0.2000, 0.2000, 0.2000])
>>> list(x.keys())
['logits']
>>> type(x.detached()).__name__, x[0].probs.shape
('Logits', torch.Size([4]))
```

### `__post_init__`

As in a dataclass, `__post_init__` runs after the generated `__init__`.
Use it to compute a default value, or to make sure that the fields are valid:

```
>>> class Batch(TensorClass):
... obs: torch.Tensor
... mask: torch.Tensor = None
...
... def __post_init__(self):
... if self.mask is None:
... self.mask = torch.ones(self.batch_size, dtype=torch.bool)
>>> b = Batch(obs=torch.zeros(3, 2), batch_size=[3])
>>> b.mask
tensor([True, True, True])
```

`__post_init__` also runs each time tensordict rebuilds an instance, that
is, makes a new instance from the data of an existing one: an index,
`clone`, `to`, `torch.stack`, `apply`, and the other operations that
return a tensorclass. It runs as well on the data that
`from_tensordict`, `from_dict` and a load (`load_memmap`, `load`)
bring in. Do little work in it, and make sure that a second run gives the
same result. In the example above, the second run finds a mask and keeps it.

On a lazy stack ([`lazy_stack()`](reference/generated/tensordict.lazy_stack.html#tensordict.lazy_stack), and the operations that
return one), `__post_init__` runs on each stacked instance, not on the
stack, so it sees fields of the shape of that instance, even when the
instances have different shapes. A lazy stack of N instances makes N calls.
The fields that it sets go to the stacked instances. `torch.stack` makes
one call, on the stacked result.

`__post_init__` does not run on the shells that tensordict builds without
fields and fills afterwards: the result of `empty()`, the tensorclass
entries of `empty(recurse=True)`, and the output of
[`pad_sequence()`](reference/generated/tensordict.pad_sequence.html#tensordict.pad_sequence). A shell has no field, not even those that
`__post_init__` would fill. Under `torch.compile`, `__post_init__`
still runs on these shells.

To validate the data once, when it comes in, set the
`skip_post_init_on_rebuild` flag. `__post_init__` then runs in the
generated `__init__`, `from_tensordict`, `from_dict`, the other
constructors (`from_any`, `from_list`, `fromkeys`, ...), and when the
data is loaded or received from another process, but not when tensordict
rebuilds an instance. Each class follows
its own flag: a tensorclass without the flag that holds one with it runs only
its own `__post_init__` on `clone()`. Subclasses inherit the flag:

```
>>> class Ragged(TensorClass["skip_post_init_on_rebuild"]):
... offsets: torch.Tensor
... indices: torch.Tensor
...
... def __post_init__(self):
... if int(self.offsets[-1]) != len(self.indices):
... raise ValueError("the last offset must be len(indices)")
>>> r = Ragged(offsets=torch.tensor([0, 2, 3]), indices=torch.zeros(3))
>>> r.clone().offsets # no check, and no device synchronization on CUDA
tensor([0, 2, 3])
```

### A custom `__init__`

If the class defines `__init__`, it replaces the generated one. When it
runs, the instance already exists, with the `batch_size`, `device`, and
`names` that the caller passed as keyword arguments. Assign the fields as
attributes. To set the batch size from the data, assign `self.batch_size`
after the fields:

```
>>> class Points(TensorClass):
... xyz: torch.Tensor
...
... def __init__(self, n: int):
... self.xyz = torch.zeros(n, 3)
... self.batch_size = [n]
>>> Points(4).batch_size
torch.Size([4])
>>> Points(4)[:2].batch_size
torch.Size([2])
```

These rules apply to a custom `__init__`:

- If it does not set a required field, the constructor raises
`TypeError: Points.__init__() did not set the required field 'xyz'`.
- Indexing, `clone`, `torch.stack`, and the other operations make new
instances without a call to `__init__`. So `__init__` must only fill
the fields, and the fields must be enough to rebuild the instance.
- As in a dataclass, a custom `__init__` does not call `__post_init__`.
If you need it, call it yourself.
- `super().__init__(...)` with fields works when the parent class is a
tensorclass with fields: it runs the generated `__init__` of the parent.
If the parent is [`TensorClass`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass) itself, a call with fields
raises `NotImplementedError`. Assign the fields instead.

### Overriding `__setattr__` and `__getitem__`

A `__setattr__` or `__getitem__` that the class defines replaces the one
of the tensorclass. For the cases that you do not handle, call the method of
`super()`. A custom `__setattr__` also runs when the constructor sets the
fields:

```
>>> class Clamped(TensorClass):
... x: torch.Tensor
...
... def __setattr__(self, key, value):
... if key == "x":
... value = value.clamp(0, 1)
... super().__setattr__(key, value)
>>> c = Clamped(x=torch.tensor([-1.0, 2.0]), batch_size=[2])
>>> c.x
tensor([0., 1.])
```

## Fields that are not tensors

A field can hold a value that is not a tensor, such as a string. The
tensorclass stores it in a wrapper.

### `NonTensorData` and `MetaData`

Two wrappers exist, and they differ when you stack instances:

- [`NonTensorData`](reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData) is the default. It keeps one value per
batch element. Stacking instances gives a
[`NonTensorStack`](reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack), and attribute access returns a list of
the values, even when all the values are equal.
- [`MetaData`](reference/generated/tensordict.MetaData.html#tensordict.MetaData) holds one value for the whole batch. Stacking
`MetaData("cfg")` with `MetaData("cfg")` returns `MetaData("cfg")`.
Stacking items with different values returns a `NonTensorStack`, as for
`NonTensorData`. Use `MetaData` for a value that is the same for every
element, such as a label or a configuration dict.

To use `MetaData`, assign a `MetaData` instance to the field:

```
>>> from tensordict import MetaData
>>> class Sample(TensorClass):
... x: torch.Tensor
... label: str
>>> a = Sample(x=torch.zeros(()), label="cfg")
>>> torch.stack([a, a]).label
LinkedList(['cfg', 'cfg'])
>>> m = Sample(x=torch.zeros(()), label=MetaData("cfg"))
>>> torch.stack([m, m]).label
'cfg'
```

`LinkedList` is a subclass of [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list). For the full rules of
non-tensor values in tensordicts, see [Non-tensor data and unbatched entries](concepts/non_tensor.html#non-tensor-data).

### Fields set to `None`

A field can be `None` at first and get a value later. The value that you
assign decides how the field is stored: a tensor is stored as a tensor, and a
string as `NonTensorData`:

```
>>> from typing import Any
>>> class Slots(TensorClass):
... X: Any
... y: Any
>>> slots = Slots(X=None, y=None, batch_size=[3, 4])
>>> slots.X = torch.ones(3, 4, 5)
>>> slots.y = "testing"
>>> print(slots)
Slots(
 X=Tensor(shape=torch.Size([3, 4, 5]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False),
 y=NonTensorData(data=testing, batch_size=torch.Size([3, 4]), device=None),
 batch_size=torch.Size([3, 4]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
```

A `None` field is a key missing from the tensor storage. Setting a field to
`None`, or deleting it with `del obj.field`, `obj.del_("field")` or
`obj.pop("field")`, removes its entry, and reading it gives `None`.
`to_dict()`, `repr` and `state_dict()` list it as `None`.

### Comparison, item assignment, and concatenation

`==` and `!=` compare two tensorclasses field by field, also the nested
ones. The result is a tensorclass with a boolean tensor for each field. For a
field that is not a tensor, the boolean tensor has the batch shape, and it is
`False` where the values differ:

```
>>> print(data == data2)
Reading(
 backup=Reading(
 count=Tensor(shape=torch.Size([3, 4, 1]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.bool, is_shared=False),
 sensor=Tensor(shape=torch.Size([3, 4]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.bool, is_shared=False),
 signal=Tensor(shape=torch.Size([3, 4, 5]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.bool, is_shared=False),
 backup=None,
 batch_size=torch.Size([3, 4]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False),
 count=Tensor(shape=torch.Size([3, 4, 1]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.bool, is_shared=False),
 sensor=Tensor(shape=torch.Size([3, 4]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.bool, is_shared=False),
 signal=Tensor(shape=torch.Size([3, 4, 5]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.bool, is_shared=False),
 batch_size=torch.Size([3, 4]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
>>> data2.sensor = "camera"
>>> (data == data2).sensor.any()
tensor(False)
```

An item assignment writes the values that are not tensors element by element,
with no warning when they differ from the rest of the batch. The field then
holds one value per element (a [`NonTensorStack`](reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorStack.html#tensordict.NonTensorStack)), and
attribute access returns a nested list of those values, with one level per
batch dimension:

```
>>> data[0] = data2[0]
>>> [row[0] for row in data.sensor]
['camera', 'lidar', 'lidar']
```

`torch.cat` and `torch.stack` keep the non-tensor value of each element.
If the inputs differ on a non-tensor field, the field of the result is a
`NonTensorStack`, and attribute access returns the nested list of values.
`torch.stack` does this even when all the inputs have the same value.
`torch.cat` of inputs that have one same value keeps that value:

```
>>> cat_tc = torch.cat([data, data2], dim=0)
>>> [row[0] for row in cat_tc.sensor]
['camera', 'lidar', 'lidar', 'camera', 'camera', 'camera']
```

## Class options

Flags change how a tensorclass converts and checks the values of its fields.
You can set them in three forms, which have the same effect:

```
>>> from tensordict import tensorclass
>>> class Foo(TensorClass["autocast"]): # bracket form
... x: int
>>> class Foo(TensorClass, autocast=True): # keyword form
... x: int
>>> @tensorclass(autocast=True) # decorator form
... class Foo:
... x: int
```

To set more than one flag, list them in the brackets:

```
>>> class Foo(TensorClass["nocast", "frozen"]):
... x: int
```

mypy rejects the bracket form. See Static type checking.

The flags are:

`autocast`

The constructor and attribute assignment convert each value to the type
annotation of its field. See Auto-casting.

`nocast`

Python numbers and NumPy arrays stay as they are. Without this flag, an
`int`, `float`, `bool`, or NumPy array becomes a tensor.

`tensor_only`

Each field must have a tensor annotation: a tensor type, a tensor collection
([`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict) or a tensorclass), or an `Optional` or
union of these. Any other annotation raises `TypeError` when the class is
defined. Python numbers and NumPy arrays become tensors. A value that cannot
become a tensor, for example a `str`, is stored as
[`NonTensorData`](reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData) with no error, and attribute access
returns the `NonTensorData` wrapper. Attribute access does not look in
the storage for non-tensor values, so it does less work. On one CPU, reading
a tensor field took 150 ns with `tensor_only` and 230 ns without it.
`benchmarks/tensorclass/test_tensorclass_speed.py` measures it.

`frozen`

Assigning a field raises [`dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html#dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError), as with
`@dataclass(frozen=True)`. See Immutability with frozen.

`shadow`

Allows field names that are members of a tensorclass, for example
`batch_size`, `device`, `names`, `sum`, `keys`, `get`, or
`to_dict`. Without this flag, such a name raises `AttributeError` when
the class is defined. A field named `data` or `fields` is allowed
without the flag, and it replaces the member of that name.

`skip_post_init_on_rebuild`

`__post_init__` runs only on the data that comes in (the generated
`__init__`, `from_tensordict`, `from_dict`, the other constructors
such as `from_any` or `fromkeys`, and loads), not each time
tensordict makes a new instance from an existing one, as in `clone`,
`to`, indexing, or `torch.stack`. See __post_init__.

`autocast`, `nocast`, and `tensor_only` are mutually exclusive. A class
with two of them raises `TypeError`.

### Auto-casting

Warning

Auto-casting is experimental. Its behavior can change in a
future release.

With `autocast`, the constructor and attribute assignment convert each value
to the annotation of its field:

- A dict becomes a [`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict), or the tensorclass of the
annotation.
- A value for an `int`, `float`, or `str` field becomes an `int`,
`float`, or `str`. For example, `torch.tensor(3)` becomes `3`.
- A value for a `torch.Tensor` field goes through [`torch.as_tensor()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.as_tensor.html#torch.as_tensor).
A value that it cannot convert, for example a `str`, raises `TypeError`.

In this example, the dict of `td` becomes a `TensorDict`, the dict of
`leaf` becomes a `Leaf`, and the tensor of `count` becomes an `int`:

```
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict
>>> class Leaf(TensorClass):
... value: torch.Tensor
>>> class Node(TensorClass["autocast"]):
... tensor: torch.Tensor
... td: TensorDict
... count: int
... leaf: Leaf
>>> node = Node(
... tensor=torch.zeros(()),
... td={"a": torch.zeros(())},
... count=torch.tensor(3),
... leaf={"value": torch.ones(())},
... )
>>> type(node.td).__name__, type(node.leaf).__name__, node.count
('TensorDict', 'Leaf', 3)
```

`update()` and `from_dict()` also convert a dict into the
`TensorDict` or tensorclass of its field. They do not convert values to
`int`, `float`, or `str`.

A field annotated with `Optional[...]`, `Union[...]`, or `A | B` is not
auto-cast. A dict that you assign to it stays a dict, because a tensorclass
can hold values that are not tensors. The other fields of the class are still
auto-cast:

```
>>> class Pair(TensorClass["autocast"]):
... left: Leaf = None
... right: Optional[Leaf] = None
>>> pair = Pair(left={"value": torch.ones(())}, right={"value": torch.ones(())})
>>> type(pair.left).__name__, type(pair.right).__name__
('Leaf', 'dict')
```

Auto-casting reads the annotations with [`typing.get_type_hints()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.get_type_hints). If one
annotation of the class does not resolve, tensordict warns
`type_hints are none, cannot perform auto-casting` and casts no field of the
class. An annotation does not resolve when it names a class that is not
visible from the module, and the annotation is a string (or the module uses
`from __future__ import annotations`). The usual case is a tensorclass that is defined
inside a function, and that another class refers to. Define such classes at
module level.

### Immutability with `frozen`

With `frozen`, assigning a field raises
[`dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html#dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError), as with `@dataclass(frozen=True)`.
The instance is also locked, so you cannot add entries to it (see
[Keys, nested keys, and locking](concepts/keys.html#keys)):

```
>>> class State(TensorClass["frozen"]):
... params: torch.Tensor
... step: torch.Tensor
>>> s = State(params=torch.zeros(3), step=torch.zeros((), dtype=torch.long))
>>> s.step = s.step + 1
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError: cannot assign to field 'step'
```

The tensors of a frozen instance are not read-only. An in-place operation on
a field, or `set_()`, writes into the existing tensor:

```
>>> _ = s.step.add_(1)
>>> s.step
tensor(1)
```

A subclass of a frozen tensorclass is frozen, with or without the flag. A
frozen class cannot subclass a tensorclass that is not frozen: this raises
`TypeError: cannot inherit frozen dataclass from a non-frozen one`. Type
checkers read a subclass without the flag as not frozen and report it, so
repeat `frozen=True` on the subclass (for mypy, see
Static type checking).

## Converting a dataclass

If you have a `@dataclass`, [`from_dataclass()`](reference/generated/tensordict.from_dataclass.html#tensordict.from_dataclass) makes a
tensorclass type or instance from it. You do not change the class definition:

```
>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> from tensordict import from_dataclass
>>> @dataclass
... class X:
... a: int
... b: torch.Tensor
>>> XTc = from_dataclass(X, autocast=True) # convert the type
>>> x_tc = from_dataclass(X(a=0, b=torch.zeros(()))) # convert an instance
>>> XTc(a=torch.tensor(1), b=torch.zeros(())).a
1
```

It accepts the flags of a tensorclass (`autocast`, `nocast`, `frozen`,
`tensor_only`, `shadow`). When it applies them (not with `dest_cls`,
and not to a type that is already a tensorclass), `autocast` with
`nocast`, or `tensor_only` with either of them on a type, emits a
`FutureWarning`. Starting with TensorDict 0.17, the default will change to
raising the `TypeError` of the decorator.

## Saving and loading

The [`memmap()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap) method saves a tensorclass instance
to a directory. Tensors are written as memory-mapped tensors, and non-tensor
values that JSON can encode are written as JSON. Other non-tensor values are
written with Python `pickle` (to an `other.pickle` file, or
`pickle.pkl` for stacked values).

[`load_memmap()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap) loads it. The result has the
original class if the loading process can import that class:

```
>>> import tempfile
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as path:
... _ = data.memmap(path)
... data_loaded = TensorDict.load_memmap(path)
... assert isinstance(data_loaded, Reading)
... assert (data_loaded == data).all()
```

The class is saved by its module and name. Another program cannot find a
class that you defined in `__main__` (a script or a notebook) under that
name. To load such data, call `load_memmap` on the class itself, for example
`Reading.load_memmap(path)`. `load_memmap` uses the class that you call it
on if its name matches the saved name.

If the saved data has pickled non-tensor values and you do not pass
`allow_pickle`, loading emits a `FutureWarning` in tensordict 0.14 and
0.15. In 0.16, the default becomes `allow_pickle=False`, which raises an
error instead of loading them. Pass `allow_pickle=True` only for data that you
trust. For the other formats, see [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving).

## Tensorclasses as module inputs and outputs

For a module whose inputs and outputs are tensorclasses, subclass
[`TensorClassModuleBase`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorClassModuleBase.html#tensordict.nn.TensorClassModuleBase). Its generic parameters declare
the input and output types for type checkers and IDEs. Its `as_td_module()`
method returns a module that you can put in a
[`TensorDictSequential`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential). See [Modules: TensorDictModule and tensordict.nn](modules.html#modules-guide) for an
example.

## `torch.compile`

Tensorclasses work with [`torch.compile()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.compile.html#torch.compile), [`torch.func`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/func.api.html#module-torch.func), and
[`torch.export.export()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/user_guide/torch_compiler/export/api_reference.html#torch.export.export). The `Particles` example at the top of this page
compiles a method with `fullgraph=True`. [torch.compile, torch.func, torch.export, and CUDA graphs](compile.html#compile) lists what makes a
function recompile or break its graph, and the workarounds. Two of them
concern tensorclasses:

- A function that returns a string field recompiles for each new string.
- A compiled function that flattens a pytree recompiles after a new
tensorclass is defined.

## Static type checking

Type checkers read the fields of a [`TensorClass`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass) subclass
as its constructor signature, as they do for a `@dataclass`. The
keyword-only `batch_size`, `device`, `names`, and `lock` arguments
follow the fields. A missing field, an unknown keyword argument, or a value of
the wrong type is an error:

```
>>> class Obs(TensorClass):
... a: torch.Tensor
... label: str = "x"
>>> obs = Obs(torch.zeros(3), batch_size=[3]) # accepted
>>> obs = Obs(a=[0.0, 1.0, 2.0], batch_size=[3]) # error: a list is not a Tensor
```

The constructor converts a list, a NumPy array, or a Python number that you
pass to a `torch.Tensor` field. A type checker expects a tensor there, so
pass `torch.as_tensor(value)`. Tensordict methods such as `reshape` and
an index return the type of the class.

The three forms of the class options differ for type checkers:

- pyright accepts the bracket form (`TensorClass["autocast"]`) and the
keyword form (`class Foo(TensorClass, autocast=True)`).
- mypy does not evaluate [`__class_getitem__()`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__class_getitem__) in a list of base
classes and rejects the bracket form. In code that mypy reads, use the
keyword form.
- Type checkers do not understand the decorator form. They know the fields of
a `@tensorclass` class, but not its tensordict methods or its
`batch_size` and `device` arguments. In code that a type checker reads,
use a subclass of `TensorClass`.

mypy reports each `frozen=True` tensorclass as "Frozen dataclass cannot
inherit from a non-frozen dataclass". These statements hold for pyright
1.1.414 and mypy 2.4.0.

## Runtime type checking

A runtime type checker that decorates a class checks the methods in its
namespace. Tensorclass marks the methods that it adds with
`__no_type_check__`, the attribute that [`typing.no_type_check()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.no_type_check) sets, so
the checkers that honor it, such as beartype and typeguard, check only the
methods written in the class body. `__init__` is not marked: it keeps the
annotations of the fields, or those of a user-defined `__init__`.

Some methods of a tensorclass have the names of builtins, such as `bool`,
`int`, `float`, `set`, and `type`. With
`from __future__ import annotations`, annotations are strings. A checker that
evaluates them in the namespace of the class finds these methods there when
the class uses the `@tensorclass` decorator, so an `int` annotation names
the method. A subclass of [`TensorClass`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass) inherits these
methods instead. With the decorator, write `builtins.int`.

## Legacy: the `@tensorclass` decorator

The [`tensorclass()`](reference/generated/tensordict.tensorclass.html#tensordict.tensorclass) decorator is the original way to declare a
tensorclass. It is kept for backward compatibility, and it is the shortest way
to convert a body of `@dataclass` code. In new code, subclass
[`TensorClass`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass) instead: it has the same behavior, and type
checkers understand it without a plugin.

```
>>> @tensorclass
... class LegacyReading:
... signal: torch.Tensor
... count: torch.Tensor
... sensor: str
... backup: Optional["LegacyReading"] = None
```

The decorator accepts each flag as a keyword argument:
`@tensorclass(autocast=True)`, `@tensorclass(frozen=True, tensor_only=True)`.

# Using TensorDict for datasets

A `torchvision` dataset applies its transform to each image again at every
epoch. The `DataLoader` reads the samples one by one to build a batch. A
[`TensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict) of memory-mapped tensors stores the converted
images once, and the `DataLoader` reads each batch from it with one index.
This tutorial does this for FashionMNIST, with the model and the training loop
of the [PyTorch Quickstart Tutorial](https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/quickstart_tutorial.html). It
is for readers who train a model from a map-style dataset.

What you will learn:

- How to convert a `torchvision` dataset into a tensordict of
[`MemoryMappedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.MemoryMappedTensor.html#tensordict.MemoryMappedTensor) entries, once.
- How to pass a tensordict to a `DataLoader` as a map-style dataset, and
why it needs `collate_fn=lambda x: x`.
- How to read the batches in a training loop.

Before you start, read [Devices and memory-mapped tensors](tensordict_memory.html#sphx-glr-tutorials-tensordict-memory-py) for
memory-mapped tensors. [Using tensorclasses for datasets](tensorclass_fashion.html#sphx-glr-tutorials-tensorclass-fashion-py) does
the same with a tensorclass.

```
import time

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from tensordict import MemoryMappedTensor, TensorDict
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from torchvision import datasets
from torchvision.transforms import ToTensor

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
print(f"Using device: {device}")
```

```
Using device: cpu
```

The `torchvision.datasets` module contains many datasets that are ready to
use. This tutorial uses FashionMNIST. Each image shows an item of clothing,
and the task is to classify the type of clothing in the image (for example
"Bag" or "Sneaker").

```
training_data = datasets.FashionMNIST(
 root="data",
 train=True,
 download=True,
 transform=ToTensor(),
)
test_data = datasets.FashionMNIST(
 root="data",
 train=False,
 download=True,
 transform=ToTensor(),
)
```

Create two tensordicts, one for the training data and one for the test
data. Their entries are memory-mapped tensors. `MemoryMappedTensor.empty`
without a file name creates an anonymous memory map: on Linux, it is in
shared memory under `/dev/shm` when it has room. To store the data in a
file on disk, pass `filename=`. The `ToTensor` transform runs once per
image, when you fill the tensordicts, and not at each epoch.

The tensordicts stay on the CPU, so that their entries stay memory-mapped
tensors. The training loop moves each batch to the device. If you pass
`device="cuda"` to the `TensorDict` constructor, the constructor copies
the whole dataset to the GPU, and the entries are no longer memory-mapped.

```
def make_memmap_tensordict(dataset):
 image_shape = dataset[0][0].squeeze().shape
 return TensorDict(
 {
 "images": MemoryMappedTensor.empty(
 (len(dataset), *image_shape), dtype=torch.float32
 ),
 "targets": MemoryMappedTensor.empty((len(dataset),), dtype=torch.int64),
 },
 batch_size=[len(dataset)],
 )

training_data_td = make_memmap_tensordict(training_data)
test_data_td = make_memmap_tensordict(test_data)
```

Fill the memory-mapped tensors. A `DataLoader` reads the dataset in
batches of 1000 images, and each batch is written into the tensordict with
one index. This step reads and converts every image once.

```
def fill(data_td, dataset):
 i = 0
 for images, targets in DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=1000): # noqa: TOR401
 n = images.shape[0]
 data_td[i : i + n] = TensorDict(
 {"images": images.squeeze(1), "targets": targets}, [n]
 )
 i += n

fill(training_data_td, training_data)
fill(test_data_td, test_data)
print(training_data_td)
```

```
TensorDict(
 fields={
 images: MemoryMappedTensor(shape=torch.Size([60000, 28, 28]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False),
 targets: MemoryMappedTensor(shape=torch.Size([60000]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.int64, is_shared=False)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([60000]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
```

## DataLoaders

Create two pairs of `DataLoader`: one pair from the `torchvision`
datasets, and one pair from the memory-mapped tensordicts.

A `TensorDict` implements `__len__`, `__getitem__`, and
`__getitems__`, so you can use it as a map-style dataset. The
`DataLoader` then reads each batch with one batched index, and the result
is already a `TensorDict`. Pass `collate_fn=lambda x: x`: the default
collate function cannot read a `TensorDict` and raises `TypeError`. If
your dataset is a list of tensordicts, pass `collate_fn=torch.stack`
instead, or `collate_fn=tensordict.lazy_stack` if their shapes differ.

```
batch_size = 64

train_dataloader = DataLoader(training_data, batch_size=batch_size) # noqa: TOR401
test_dataloader = DataLoader(test_data, batch_size=batch_size) # noqa: TOR401

train_dataloader_td = DataLoader( # noqa: TOR401
 training_data_td, batch_size=batch_size, collate_fn=lambda x: x
)
test_dataloader_td = DataLoader( # noqa: TOR401
 test_data_td, batch_size=batch_size, collate_fn=lambda x: x
)
```

Each batch of the tensordict `DataLoader` is a `TensorDict` with
`batch_size=[64]`:

```
print(next(iter(train_dataloader_td)))
```

```
TensorDict(
 fields={
 images: Tensor(shape=torch.Size([64, 28, 28]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False),
 targets: Tensor(shape=torch.Size([64]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.int64, is_shared=False)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([64]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
```

Time one pass over the training data with each data loader, without a
model. This measures the data loading alone:

```
def time_one_pass(dataloader):
 t0 = time.perf_counter()
 for _ in dataloader:
 pass
 return time.perf_counter() - t0

print(f"torchvision DataLoader: {time_one_pass(train_dataloader):.2f} s")
print(f"TensorDict DataLoader: {time_one_pass(train_dataloader_td):.2f} s")
```

```
torchvision DataLoader: 2.11 s
TensorDict DataLoader: 0.09 s
```

## Model

The model is the same as in the
[Quickstart Tutorial](https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/quickstart_tutorial.html).

```
class Net(nn.Module):
 def __init__(self):
 super().__init__()
 self.flatten = nn.Flatten()
 self.linear_relu_stack = nn.Sequential(
 nn.Linear(28 * 28, 512),
 nn.ReLU(),
 nn.Linear(512, 512),
 nn.ReLU(),
 nn.Linear(512, 10),
 )

 def forward(self, x):
 x = self.flatten(x)
 logits = self.linear_relu_stack(x)
 return logits

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = Net().to(device)
model_td = Net().to(device)
model_td.load_state_dict(model.state_dict())
```

```
<All keys matched successfully>
```

## Optimizing the parameters

Optimize the parameters of the model with stochastic gradient descent and
the cross-entropy loss. Both models start from the same parameters.

```
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
optimizer_td = torch.optim.SGD(model_td.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

def train(dataloader, model, loss_fn, optimizer):
 size = len(dataloader.dataset)
 model.train()

 for batch, (X, y) in enumerate(dataloader):
 X, y = X.to(device), y.to(device)

 pred = model(X)
 loss = loss_fn(pred, y)

 optimizer.zero_grad()
 loss.backward()
 optimizer.step()

 if batch % 300 == 0:
 loss, current = loss.item(), batch * len(X)
 print(f"loss: {loss:>7f} [{current:>5d}/{size:>5d}]")
```

The training loop for the `TensorDict` data loader reads the images and
the targets by key, and moves them to the device.

```
def train_td(dataloader, model, loss_fn, optimizer):
 size = len(dataloader.dataset)
 model.train()

 for batch, data in enumerate(dataloader):
 X, y = data["images"].to(device), data["targets"].to(device)

 pred = model(X)
 loss = loss_fn(pred, y)

 optimizer.zero_grad()
 loss.backward()
 optimizer.step()

 if batch % 300 == 0:
 loss, current = loss.item(), batch * len(X)
 print(f"loss: {loss:>7f} [{current:>5d}/{size:>5d}]")

def test(dataloader, model, loss_fn):
 size = len(dataloader.dataset)
 num_batches = len(dataloader)
 model.eval()
 test_loss, correct = 0, 0
 with torch.no_grad():
 for X, y in dataloader:
 X, y = X.to(device), y.to(device)

 pred = model(X)

 test_loss += loss_fn(pred, y).item()
 correct += (pred.argmax(1) == y).type(torch.float).sum().item()

 test_loss /= num_batches
 correct /= size

 print(
 f"Test Error: \n Accuracy: {(100 * correct):>0.1f}%, Avg loss: {test_loss:>8f} \n"
 )

def test_td(dataloader, model, loss_fn):
 size = len(dataloader.dataset)
 num_batches = len(dataloader)
 model.eval()
 test_loss, correct = 0, 0
 with torch.no_grad():
 for batch in dataloader:
 X, y = batch["images"].to(device), batch["targets"].to(device)

 pred = model(X)

 test_loss += loss_fn(pred, y).item()
 correct += (pred.argmax(1) == y).type(torch.float).sum().item()

 test_loss /= num_batches
 correct /= size

 print(
 f"Test Error: \n Accuracy: {(100 * correct):>0.1f}%, Avg loss: {test_loss:>8f} \n"
 )
```

Train each model for one epoch, and test it once. The first run uses the
`TensorDict` data loaders, the second run uses the `torchvision` data
loaders.

```
epochs = 1

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for t in range(epochs):
 print(f"Epoch {t + 1}\n-------------------------")
 train_td(train_dataloader_td, model_td, loss_fn, optimizer_td)
 test_td(test_dataloader_td, model_td, loss_fn)
print(f"TensorDict training done! time: {time.perf_counter() - t0: 4.4f} s")

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for t in range(epochs):
 print(f"Epoch {t + 1}\n-------------------------")
 train(train_dataloader, model, loss_fn, optimizer)
 test(test_dataloader, model, loss_fn)
print(f"Training done! time: {time.perf_counter() - t0: 4.4f} s")
```

## Conclusion

You can now convert a dataset into a tensordict of memory-mapped tensors
once. Then you train a model from it with a `DataLoader` and
`collate_fn=lambda x: x`.

The two training runs use the same model, the same initial parameters, and
the same optimizer, so their times differ only by the data loading. The
one-pass timings before the training show the data loading alone. The
`torchvision` data loader applies `ToTensor` to each image, and collates
64 samples into each batch. The `TensorDict` data loader reads each batch
from the memory-mapped tensors with one index. The times above come from
the machine that built this page. They depend on the hardware and on the
load of the machine, so measure them on your own machine.

# Exporting tensordict modules

**Author**: [Vincent Moens](https://github.com/vmoens)

After you write a model with `tensordict.nn`, you can export its
computational graph with [`torch.export.export()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/user_guide/torch_compiler/export/api_reference.html#torch.export.export). The exported program
takes and returns plain tensors, and it does not need tensordict at run time.
Use it to run the model on other hardware (robots, drones, edge devices), or
to remove the dependency on tensordict. This tutorial is for readers who
deploy a `tensordict.nn` model.

What you will learn:

- How to call a `tensordict.nn` module with tensors instead of a
[`TensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict).
- How to export the module with `torch.export` and save the result to a file.
- How to export a module that reads and writes nested keys.
- How to select the outputs of the model before you export it.

Before you start, read the [TensorDictModule](tensordict_module.html#tensordictmodule)
tutorial.

```
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import torch
from tensordict.nn import (
 NormalParamExtractor,
 TensorDictModule as Mod,
 TensorDictSequential as Seq,
)
from torch import nn
```

## Building the model

Build a small network with `tensordict.nn`. The network has:

- A linear layer that maps the input to a hidden representation.
- A ReLU activation.
- A second linear layer that writes a latent representation.

A [`NormalParamExtractor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.nn.distributions.NormalParamExtractor.html#tensordict.nn.distributions.NormalParamExtractor) then splits the latent
tensor into two outputs, `"loc"` and `"scale"`.

```
model = Seq(
 # 1. A small network for embedding
 Mod(nn.Linear(3, 4), in_keys=["x"], out_keys=["hidden"]),
 Mod(nn.ReLU(), in_keys=["hidden"], out_keys=["hidden"]),
 Mod(nn.Linear(4, 4), in_keys=["hidden"], out_keys=["latent"]),
 # 2. Extracting params (splits into loc and scale)
 Mod(NormalParamExtractor(), in_keys=["latent"], out_keys=["loc", "scale"]),
)
```

Run the model with a tensor as a keyword argument, and look at the output:

```
torch.manual_seed(0)
x = torch.randn(1, 3)
print(model(x=x))
```

```
(tensor([[0.0000, 0.8067, 0.0791, 0.0000]], grad_fn=<ReluBackward0>), tensor([[-0.1955, 0.2908, -0.2976, 0.2212]], grad_fn=<AddmmBackward0>), tensor([[-0.1955, 0.2908]], grad_fn=<SplitBackward0>), tensor([[0.8236, 1.1446]], grad_fn=<ClampMinBackward0>))
```

Called with a tensor, the model returns one tensor per output key: here
`"hidden"`, `"latent"`, `"loc"`, and `"scale"`. For a large model,
you usually need fewer outputs. The section "Selecting the outputs" below
shows how to keep only some of them.

## Using `torch.export` with a `TensorDictModule`

`torch.export` captures the graph of a module in a standard form, which
does not depend on `tensordict`. The [`export()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/user_guide/torch_compiler/export/api_reference.html#torch.export.export)
function returns an `ExportedProgram`, which has these attributes:

- `graph_module`: the FX graph that `export` captured.
- `graph_signature`: the inputs and outputs of the graph.
- `module()`: a method that returns a callable, which you can use in
place of the original module.

The model accepts positional and keyword arguments. This tutorial uses
keyword arguments, because they name the input keys.

```
from torch.export import export

model_export = export(model, args=(), kwargs={"x": x})
```

Look at the module:

```
print("module:", model_export.module())
```

```
module: GraphModule(
 (module): Module(
 (0): Module(
 (module): Module()
 )
 (2): Module(
 (module): Module()
 )
 )
 (_guards_fn): GuardsFn()
)

def forward(self, x):
 x, = fx_pytree.tree_flatten_spec(([], {'x':x}), self._in_spec)
 module_0_module_weight = getattr(self.module, "0").module.weight
 module_0_module_bias = getattr(self.module, "0").module.bias
 module_2_module_weight = getattr(self.module, "2").module.weight
 module_2_module_bias = getattr(self.module, "2").module.bias
 _guards_fn = self._guards_fn(x); _guards_fn = None
 linear = torch.ops.aten.linear.default(x, module_0_module_weight, module_0_module_bias); x = module_0_module_weight = module_0_module_bias = None
 relu = torch.ops.aten.relu.default(linear); linear = None
 linear_1 = torch.ops.aten.linear.default(relu, module_2_module_weight, module_2_module_bias); module_2_module_weight = module_2_module_bias = None
 chunk = torch.ops.aten.chunk.default(linear_1, 2, -1)
 getitem = chunk[0]
 getitem_1 = chunk[1]; chunk = None
 add = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(getitem_1, 0.5254586935043335); getitem_1 = None
 softplus = torch.ops.aten.softplus.default(add); add = None
 add_1 = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(softplus, 0.01); softplus = None
 clamp_min = torch.ops.aten.clamp_min.default(add_1, 0.0001); add_1 = None
 return pytree.tree_unflatten((relu, linear_1, getitem, clamp_min), self._out_spec)

# To see more debug info, please use `graph_module.print_readable()`
```

You call this module like the original module, and it returns the same
tensors:

```
exported = model_export.module()
for out_model, out_exported in zip(model(x=x), exported(x=x)):
 torch.testing.assert_close(out_model, out_exported)
```

Export does not optimize the graph. The exported module runs the same tensor
operations as the original module, one by one, without the tensordict reads
and writes. To make it faster, compile it (see [torch.compile, torch.func, torch.export, and CUDA graphs](../compile.html#compile)), or compile
it ahead of time with AOTInductor (see "Further reading").

Print the FX graph:

```
print(model_export.graph_module.print_readable(print_output=False))
```

```
class GraphModule(torch.nn.Module):
 def forward(self, p_module_0_module_weight: "f32[4, 3]", p_module_0_module_bias: "f32[4]", p_module_2_module_weight: "f32[4, 4]", p_module_2_module_bias: "f32[4]", x: "f32[1, 3]"):
 # File: /__w/tensordict/tensordict/env/lib/python3.12/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/linear.py:134 in forward, code: return F.linear(input, self.weight, self.bias)
 linear: "f32[1, 4]" = torch.ops.aten.linear.default(x, p_module_0_module_weight, p_module_0_module_bias); x = p_module_0_module_weight = p_module_0_module_bias = None

 # File: /__w/tensordict/tensordict/env/lib/python3.12/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/activation.py:143 in forward, code: return F.relu(input, inplace=self.inplace)
 relu: "f32[1, 4]" = torch.ops.aten.relu.default(linear); linear = None

 # File: /__w/tensordict/tensordict/env/lib/python3.12/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/linear.py:134 in forward, code: return F.linear(input, self.weight, self.bias)
 linear_1: "f32[1, 4]" = torch.ops.aten.linear.default(relu, p_module_2_module_weight, p_module_2_module_bias); p_module_2_module_weight = p_module_2_module_bias = None

 # File: /__w/tensordict/tensordict/tensordict/nn/distributions/continuous.py:80 in forward, code: loc, scale = tensor.chunk(2, -1)
 chunk = torch.ops.aten.chunk.default(linear_1, 2, -1)
 getitem: "f32[1, 2]" = chunk[0]
 getitem_1: "f32[1, 2]" = chunk[1]; chunk = None

 # File: /__w/tensordict/tensordict/tensordict/nn/utils.py:96 in forward, code: return torch.nn.functional.softplus(x + self.bias) + self.min_val
 add: "f32[1, 2]" = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(getitem_1, 0.5254586935043335); getitem_1 = None
 softplus: "f32[1, 2]" = torch.ops.aten.softplus.default(add); add = None
 add_1: "f32[1, 2]" = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(softplus, 0.01); softplus = None

 # File: /__w/tensordict/tensordict/tensordict/nn/distributions/continuous.py:81 in forward, code: scale = self.scale_mapping(scale).clamp_min(self.scale_lb)
 clamp_min: "f32[1, 2]" = torch.ops.aten.clamp_min.default(add_1, 0.0001); add_1 = None
 return (relu, linear_1, getitem, clamp_min)
```

### Working with nested keys

Nested keys are tuples of strings, such as `("some", "key")`. A keyword
argument must be a single string, so [`dispatch`](../reference/generated/tensordict.nn.dispatch.html#tensordict.nn.dispatch)
joins the parts of a nested key with an underscore (`"_"`). In the
example below, the input key `("some", "key")` becomes the keyword
argument `some_key`.

```
model_nested = Seq(
 Mod(lambda x: x + 1, in_keys=[("some", "key")], out_keys=["hidden"]),
 Mod(lambda x: x - 1, in_keys=["hidden"], out_keys=[("some", "output")]),
).select_out_keys(("some", "output"))

model_nested_export = export(model_nested, args=(), kwargs={"some_key": x})
print("exported module with nested input:", model_nested_export.module())
```

```
exported module with nested input: GraphModule(
 (_guards_fn): GuardsFn()
)

def forward(self, some_key):
 some_key, = fx_pytree.tree_flatten_spec(([], {'some_key':some_key}), self._in_spec)
 _guards_fn = self._guards_fn(some_key); _guards_fn = None
 add = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(some_key, 1); some_key = None
 sub = torch.ops.aten.sub.Tensor(add, 1); add = None
 return pytree.tree_unflatten((sub,), self._out_spec)

# To see more debug info, please use `graph_module.print_readable()`
```

The `forward` method of the exported module takes `some_key`:

```
out = model_nested_export.module()(some_key=x)
torch.testing.assert_close(out, x)
```

The callable that `module()` returns is a plain Python callable. You can
compile it with [`compile()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.compile.html#torch.compile).

### Saving the exported module

`torch.export` has its own file format. Save the program with
[`save()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/user_guide/torch_compiler/export/api_reference.html#torch.export.save) and load it with [`load()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/user_guide/torch_compiler/export/api_reference.html#torch.export.load). By
convention, the file name ends with `".pt2"`:

```
path = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "model.pt2"
torch.export.save(model_export, path)
model_loaded = torch.export.load(path)
for out_model, out_loaded in zip(model(x=x), model_loaded.module()(x=x)):
 torch.testing.assert_close(out_model, out_loaded)
```

## Selecting the outputs

By default, a `tensordict.nn` module keeps every intermediate value in its
output. During training, you can log these values, or rebuild a
distribution from its saved parameters instead of saving the
[`Distribution`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributions.html#torch.distributions.distribution.Distribution) object. The extra memory is small
during training, because autograd keeps these tensors for the backward pass
anyway.

An exported inference model usually needs one or two outputs. Select them
before you export, so that the exported graph returns only these tensors.
You can select outputs in three ways:

1. Pass the `selected_out_keys` keyword argument when you build the
[`TensorDictSequential`](../reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential).
2. Call the [`select_out_keys()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModuleBase.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModuleBase.select_out_keys) method.
It changes the `out_keys` attribute in place. To undo it, call
[`reset_out_keys()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModuleBase.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModuleBase.reset_out_keys).
3. Wrap the module in a [`TensorDictSequential`](../reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential) that
selects the keys:

```
>>> module_filtered = Seq(module, selected_out_keys=["loc"])
```

Select the `"loc"` output with the second method. With an `x` input,
the model now returns one tensor, the `"loc"` output:

```
model.select_out_keys("loc")
print(model(x=x))
```

```
tensor([[-0.1955, 0.2908]], grad_fn=<SplitBackward0>)
```

Export the model again. The graph now returns a single tensor:

```
model_export = export(model, args=(), kwargs={"x": x})
print("module:", model_export.module())
```

```
module: GraphModule(
 (module): Module(
 (0): Module(
 (module): Module()
 )
 (2): Module(
 (module): Module()
 )
 )
 (_guards_fn): GuardsFn()
)

def forward(self, x):
 x, = fx_pytree.tree_flatten_spec(([], {'x':x}), self._in_spec)
 module_0_module_weight = getattr(self.module, "0").module.weight
 module_0_module_bias = getattr(self.module, "0").module.bias
 module_2_module_weight = getattr(self.module, "2").module.weight
 module_2_module_bias = getattr(self.module, "2").module.bias
 _guards_fn = self._guards_fn(x); _guards_fn = None
 linear = torch.ops.aten.linear.default(x, module_0_module_weight, module_0_module_bias); x = module_0_module_weight = module_0_module_bias = None
 relu = torch.ops.aten.relu.default(linear); linear = None
 linear_1 = torch.ops.aten.linear.default(relu, module_2_module_weight, module_2_module_bias); relu = module_2_module_weight = module_2_module_bias = None
 chunk = torch.ops.aten.chunk.default(linear_1, 2, -1); linear_1 = None
 getitem = chunk[0]
 getitem_1 = chunk[1]; chunk = None
 add = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(getitem_1, 0.5254586935043335); getitem_1 = None
 softplus = torch.ops.aten.softplus.default(add); add = None
 add_1 = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(softplus, 0.01); softplus = None
 clamp_min = torch.ops.aten.clamp_min.default(add_1, 0.0001); add_1 = clamp_min = None
 return pytree.tree_unflatten((getitem,), self._out_spec)

# To see more debug info, please use `graph_module.print_readable()`
```

## Conclusion

You can now export a `tensordict.nn` model with `torch.export` into a
program that takes and returns plain tensors. You can pass nested keys as
keyword arguments joined with `"_"`, and save the program to a `.pt2`
file and load it again. You can also select the outputs of the model before
the export.

# Functional calls and ensembles with TensorDict

**Author**: [Vincent Moens](https://github.com/vmoens)

The parameters of a [`Module`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Module.html#torch.nn.Module) form a tree of named tensors,
which a [`TensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict) holds with the same structure. With
the parameters in a tensordict, one call replaces all the parameters of a
module, stacks the parameters of several models, or passes them to
[`torch.func`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/func.api.html#module-torch.func). This tutorial is for readers who train ensembles of
models, or who swap the parameters of a model at run time.

What you will learn:

- How to extract the parameters of a module with
[`from_module()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict.from_module), and swap them with
[`to_module()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_module.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_module).
- How to run an ensemble of models with [`torch.vmap()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.vmap.html#torch.vmap) over a stack of
parameters.
- How to stack the parameters of several modules with
[`from_modules()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_modules.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_modules), and how
[`EnsembleModule`](../reference/generated/tensordict.nn.EnsembleModule.html#tensordict.nn.EnsembleModule) does it for you.
- How to call [`torch.func.functional_call()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.functional_call.html#torch.func.functional_call) with these parameters.

Before you start, read [Getting, setting, and nesting keys](tensordict_keys.html#sphx-glr-tutorials-tensordict-keys-py) for nested
keys.

## TensorDict as a parameter container

[`from_module()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict.from_module) copies the references to the
parameters and buffers of a module into a nested
[`TensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict). The structure of the tensordict is the
structure of the module.

```
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from tensordict import TensorDict

torch.manual_seed(0)
module = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 4), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(4, 1))
params = TensorDict.from_module(module)
print(params)
```

```
TensorDict(
 fields={
 0: TensorDict(
 fields={
 bias: Parameter(shape=torch.Size([4]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False),
 weight: Parameter(shape=torch.Size([4, 3]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False),
 2: TensorDict(
 fields={
 bias: Parameter(shape=torch.Size([1]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False),
 weight: Parameter(shape=torch.Size([1, 4]), device=cpu, dtype=torch.float32, is_shared=False)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)},
 batch_size=torch.Size([]),
 device=None,
 is_shared=False)
```

The [`TensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict) holds the same
[`Parameter`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.parameter.Parameter.html#torch.nn.parameter.Parameter) objects as the module. Tensordict operations
apply to all of them at once. For example, this line makes a copy of all
the parameters, with zeros as values:

```
params_zero = params.detach().clone().zero_()
print("All zeros:", (params_zero == 0).all())
```

```
All zeros: True
```

## Swapping parameters with a context manager

[`to_module()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_module.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_module) replaces the parameters of a module
with the values of the tensordict. Used in a `with` block, it puts the
original parameters back at the end of the block.

```
x = torch.randn(5, 3)

with params_zero.to_module(module):
 y_zero = module(x)

print("Output with zeroed params:", y_zero)
assert (y_zero == 0).all()

y_original = module(x)
print("Output with original params:", y_original)
assert not (y_original == 0).all()
```

```
Output with zeroed params: tensor([[0.],
 [0.],
 [0.],
 [0.],
 [0.]], grad_fn=<AddmmBackward0>)
Output with original params: tensor([[-0.0624],
 [ 0.0916],
 [ 0.2135],
 [ 0.1337],
 [ 0.1770]], grad_fn=<AddmmBackward0>)
```

## Model ensembling with `torch.vmap`

You can stack parameter tensordicts like any tensordict. The stack has a
batch dimension, with one element per set of parameters.
[`vmap()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.vmap.html#torch.vmap) then runs the model with each set of parameters in one
vectorized call.

```
params_ones = params.detach().clone().apply_(lambda t: t.fill_(1.0))
params_stack = torch.stack([params_zero, params_ones, params])

print("Stacked params batch_size:", params_stack.batch_size)

def call(x, td):
 with td.to_module(module):
 return module(x)

x = torch.randn(3, 5, 3)
y = torch.vmap(call)(x, params_stack)
print("Output shape:", y.shape)

assert (y[0] == 0).all()
```

```
Stacked params batch_size: torch.Size([3])
Output shape: torch.Size([3, 5, 1])
```

## Stacking the parameters of several modules

An ensemble usually has several copies of a model, each with its own random
initialization. [`from_modules()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_modules.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_modules) stacks the
parameters of several modules with the same structure into one tensordict.
The first dimension of the result is the index of the module:

```
modules = [nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 4), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(4, 1)) for _ in range(3)]
ensemble_params = TensorDict.from_modules(*modules)
print("Ensemble params batch_size:", ensemble_params.batch_size)
```

```
Ensemble params batch_size: torch.Size([3])
```

Use one of the modules as the structure, and run it with each set of
parameters. `in_dims=(None, 0)` gives the same input `x` to every
model, and maps over the first dimension of the parameters:

```
x = torch.randn(5, 3)
y = torch.vmap(call, in_dims=(None, 0))(x, ensemble_params)
print("Output shape:", y.shape)
for i, member in enumerate(modules):
 torch.testing.assert_close(y[i], member(x))
```

```
Output shape: torch.Size([3, 5, 1])
```

To train the stacked parameters, pass `as_module=True`. The result is a
[`TensorDictParams`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictParams.html#tensordict.TensorDictParams), a tensordict that is also an
[`Module`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Module.html#torch.nn.Module), so that an optimizer can find its parameters
with `parameters()`.

For a [`TensorDictModule`](../reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule),
[`EnsembleModule`](../reference/generated/tensordict.nn.EnsembleModule.html#tensordict.nn.EnsembleModule) does all of this in one step. It
makes `num_copies` copies of the module with new random parameters, and
adds a leading dimension of size `num_copies` to its input and outputs:

```
from tensordict.nn import EnsembleModule, TensorDictModule

member = TensorDictModule(nn.Linear(3, 1), in_keys=["x"], out_keys=["y"])
ensemble = EnsembleModule(member, num_copies=4)
out = ensemble(TensorDict({"x": torch.randn(5, 3)}, batch_size=[5]))
print("EnsembleModule output batch_size:", out.batch_size)
```

```
EnsembleModule output batch_size: torch.Size([4, 5])
```

## Functional calls with `torch.func`

[`functional_call()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.functional_call.html#torch.func.functional_call) takes a `dict` of parameters, with the
names of a state dict as keys. `flatten_keys(".")` turns the nested keys of
the tensordict into these names, and `dict(...items())` turns the result
into a `dict`:

```
from torch.func import functional_call

flat_params = params.flatten_keys(".")
state_dict = dict(flat_params.items())
x = torch.randn(5, 3)
y = functional_call(module, state_dict, x)
print("functional_call output:", y.shape)
```

```
functional_call output: torch.Size([5, 1])
```

## Conclusion

You can now extract the parameters of a module into a
[`TensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict) with `from_module`. `to_module` swaps
them for the length of a `with` block. You can stack parameters by
hand or with `from_modules`, and run the whole ensemble in one
[`torch.vmap()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.vmap.html#torch.vmap) call. [`EnsembleModule`](../reference/generated/tensordict.nn.EnsembleModule.html#tensordict.nn.EnsembleModule) builds such
an ensemble in one step. `flatten_keys(".")` gives the parameter names
that [`torch.func.functional_call()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.functional_call.html#torch.func.functional_call) expects.

## Further reading

- [torch.compile, torch.func, torch.export, and CUDA graphs](../compile.html#compile) explains how tensordicts work with [`torch.func`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/func.api.html#module-torch.func),
including per-sample gradients with [`torch.vmap()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.vmap.html#torch.vmap).
- [Modules: TensorDictModule and tensordict.nn](../modules.html#modules-guide) explains [`TensorDictParams`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictParams.html#tensordict.TensorDictParams) and
the other modules of `tensordict.nn`.
- [Building models with TensorDictModule](tensordict_module.html#sphx-glr-tutorials-tensordict-module-py) shows how to build models
from [`TensorDictModule`](../reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule).
- [tensordict.nn](../reference/nn.html#api-nn) lists all the classes of `tensordict.nn`.

# Tutorials

Each tutorial solves one task with a script that runs from top to bottom on a
CPU. The documentation build runs every script, so the output on each page
comes from the code above it. Each page has links to download the script and
a Jupyter notebook, and ends with a "Further reading" list of the guides and
API pages that go deeper. If you are new to tensordict, read
[Getting started](../getting_started.html#getting-started) first.

The sidebar lists the tutorials in four groups, in reading order:

- Basics: keys, indexing, shapes, row-by-row filling, and lazy stacks of
streamed data.
- Storage: devices and memory-mapped tensors, the zarr backend, and a
benchmark of the serialization formats.
- tensordict.nn: modules that read and write tensordicts, functional calls and
ensembles, and export with `torch.export`.
- Data loading: datasets in a `TensorDict` or a `TensorClass`, and batched
loading of an image dataset.
